stories.Headline: OpenAI kicks off charm offensive to change voters’ view of data centres
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on Nov 5 a set of policies meant to win local support for data centers, in the works since August and released just after the US midterm elections. The company said it will stop using non-disclosure agreements with public officials when it negotiates or discusses future sites, though proprietary information will stay confidential. It will also give residents access to construction plans and the likely effects on traffic, noise and lighting. Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer, said the centers will provide ongoing work because the hardware inside must be updated every three to five years. He added that one OpenAI facility in southern Ohio is expected to create 2,500 long-term jobs with an average annual salary of US$80,000 (S$102,000).

The announcement followed a rough week for the industry at the ballot box. Of the 41 data center-related ballot measures voted on this week, all but one went against data centers, according to Ballotpedia. Seven municipalities passed permanent bans on new data centers, and ten others voted to cap construction by size or electrical footprint. Defiance, Ohio, approved a ban on new centers needing more than 25 megawatts by 63% to 37%, while 77% of voters in Edgewater, Florida, and 82% in Alhambra, California, backed outright bans. Bloomington, Illinois, and Peru and Wiscasset in Maine approved moratoriums, and in Wilmington, Ohio, eight in ten voters rejected a rural rezoning that would have paved the way for a new center.

Democrats also flipped governorships in Texas, Georgia and Ohio with candidates who promised to pause new data center permits and tighten construction rules. Shares of data center operators and power companies tumbled on Nov 4 as investors bet the results could bring tougher permitting, higher costs and slower building. OpenAI president Greg Brockman said at a separate event on Nov 4 that the industry needs to do a better job explaining to local communities why data centers can help them. Lehane described the new projects as unlike the older idea of a black box in a pasture that gave little to its neighbors, and he noted that partners such as Oracle build and own much of OpenAI's data center infrastructure, with the capacity dedicated to the start-up. Elon Musk, who reportedly gave $224 million to Republican candidates in Texas, wrote on X that data centers in space looked pretty appealing.

The vote reflects public attitudes that were already visible before the election. A June survey by Reuters and Ipsos found that only 14% of Americans would support a data center being built near them. OpenAI's leaders have spent two years building ties with President Donald Trump's administration to shape federal AI policy, and Sam Altman gave US$1 million to Trump's inaugural committee, while Brockman gave US$25 million to a Trump super PAC in 2025. Asked how the company would answer skepticism from Democrats, Lehane pointed to his long experience in the party, including serving as a top lawyer and spokesperson in the Clinton administration and as press secretary to Al Gore during his presidential run. The articles do not say how communities will respond to the new policies.

stories.Headline: Is AI Taking White-Collar Jobs? What the Latest Numbers Tell Us
stories.Summary:
Fearing that artificial intelligence will soon disrupt their fields, a growing number of white-collar workers are voluntarily leaving established careers, according to a Guardian report published on November 6, 2026. The article points to Mrinank Sharma, an AI researcher who quit Anthropic earlier that year and warned in a widely viewed resignation letter of a world "in peril," and says he plans to pursue a poetry degree. Other workers across tech, public relations and consulting say AI changed the substance and stability of their jobs, and some are shifting to very different work. The reporting describes these moves as a response to forecasted disruption rather than to any confirmed wave of layoffs.

The article notes that economic data so far does not show AI has caused widespread job losses, citing an Economist estimate that the technology has created about 1 million US jobs against roughly 200,000 layoffs attributed to it. Even so, a Pew Research Center survey found that 71 percent of Americans believe AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years. The workers profiled describe a range of pressures, including burnout, uncertainty about career ladders, and being pushed to adopt AI tools that some felt were legally or creatively problematic. Several said their roles had shifted toward managing AI output and away from the work they were hired to do.

Among those interviewed, Vanessa Hsia, 30, left a near-decade in public relations to seek a master's degree in comparative literature, while Hanna Horvath, 29, left her editing job at Bankrate to freelance and work as a financial planner. A former software engineer, who asked to remain anonymous, said his career had "completely changed" as AI automated coding, and Chris, another former engineer, joined a major east coast police department last year. Kara, a former advertising producer, moved toward acting and work as a barista, describing the change as making her feel "spiritually lighter." The article quotes the workers themselves, several of whom asked to use pseudonyms for fear of retribution.

The article places these choices against predictions from AI executives, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who in May 2025 forecast that AI would displace half of entry-level white-collar jobs by the end of the decade, a prediction the article says has not yet materialized. It cites Notre Dame economist Brendan Moore, who argues that worker fears may stem from executive warnings and from companies citing AI in layoffs, and who warns that even fear alone could ripple through wages and growth, as happened during the Covid-era "great resignation." It also reports that Senator Bernie Sanders introduced a bill calling for a federal moratorium on new AI datacenters until worker safeguards are in place. The article ends with Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg's view that the industry's doom-laden rhetoric is puzzling, while the workers quoted say the instability is already real for them.

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] Agoda and OpenAI Bring AI Learning to Life
stories.Summary:
Agoda, the digital travel platform, hosted the 12th edition of its Agoda Tech Camp Day on November 5 and 6, 2026, in Bangkok, welcoming more than 420 students from four Thai universities. This edition was run with OpenAI and brings the program's total reach to over 4,100 students since 2023. Workshops introduced students to basic AI concepts and to practical uses of ChatGPT for their studies and future careers, drawing on examples from Agoda's own work. The program was framed around the finding from Agoda's AI Developer Report 2026 that junior developers were nearly three times as likely as senior developers to name a lack of skills as a barrier to wider AI agent adoption.

During the workshops, students compared Chat mode with Work mode in ChatGPT and used personal instructions, tools and skills to guide an agent through multi-step tasks. Among the projects, they turned spreadsheet data into a presentation and an interactive web app, and they built and published their own applications. They also learned to package workflow instructions into reusable skills so an agent could repeat a set of steps from one prompt. Participating students will receive two months of ChatGPT Plus access to keep practicing after the event. The students came from first to fourth year at Sripatum University, Rajamangala University of Technology Phra Nakhon, Rajamangala University of Technology Thanyaburi and Suan Sunandha Rajabhat University.

Agoda's Chief Technology Officer, Idan Zalzberg, said that AI is most useful when people understand its abilities and limits and can apply it to a problem they care about. He said the event shares Agoda's practical experience with future tech talent and, through OpenAI, adds expertise in building AI, helping students use it responsibly. Sandy Kunvatanagarn, OpenAI's Head of Policy for ASEAN, said Thai students are already curious about AI and that the goal is to build their confidence and judgment, including checking sources and questioning output. Dr. Preesan Rakwatin of the Digital Economy Promotion Agency attended the opening ceremony and said that building AI skills is essential for Thailand's young people and its digital economy. Government support also came alongside the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation and the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration.

The companies present the event against a backdrop of strong AI use in Thailand, which ranks among the top 20 countries for weekly active ChatGPT users. According to OpenAI's internal data, creative media, writing and communication, and education and learning are the three most common ChatGPT uses among 18- to 24-year-olds there. Agoda says the program fits Thailand's push for AI adoption, which it links to productivity, growth and new jobs, and it points to the company's engineering teams in Thailand as part of that effort. Since launching, Agoda Tech Camp Day has also covered UX/UI design and web development for high school and university students, with workshops led by Agoda engineers. The release does not describe any specific plans beyond the current event.

stories.Headline: Digital Realty backs NextDC, opens Latin American AI lab in global push
stories.Summary:
Digital Realty, the cloud and carrier-neutral data center company based in Austin, Texas, announced on November 5, 2026 that it has opened its first Digital Realty Innovation Lab in Latin America. The lab sits at the company's Vinhedo II campus in São Paulo, Brazil, and gives customers a live data center setting in which to test and validate multi-vendor artificial intelligence infrastructure before deploying it at scale. The São Paulo site follows earlier labs in Northern Virginia, Tokyo and London. Digital Realty says the lab lets customers see how different components work together before they commit to an architecture.

The São Paulo lab is built for high-density AI workloads, with liquid-cooled racks supporting cabinet densities of 150 kilowatts and above. It offers chilled-water cooling, containment, and both liquid-to-liquid and air-to-liquid configurations so customers can compare cooling approaches. The facility includes a distributed redundant design, parallel uninterrupted power supply architecture, dual diverse fiber entry paths and a carrier-neutral design. It also includes integrated building management and electrical power monitoring, along with multi-layer physical, network and operational security. The company says these features help customers make more informed decisions about cost of ownership, scalability and resilience.

Claude Brown, Senior Vice President of American Sales at Digital Realty, said that AI infrastructure is changing quickly enough to make interoperability harder, and that customers need confidence components will perform at scale. Chris Torto, founder and chief executive of Ascenty, said the lab is an investment in the future of AI in Latin America, backed by years of local infrastructure work. Partners including CommScope, Nokia, OpenGlobe and Oracle issued statements supporting the lab, with Oracle describing a jointly validated architecture for Exadata Cloud@Customer. Digital Realty also named several build partners, including EBM, IDS, Multiway, Consultimer, Schneider Electric and Delta.

Digital Realty plans to keep expanding its network of innovation labs, with sites in Singapore and Johannesburg planned for late 2026. The company describes its global footprint as more than 300 facilities in over 55 metros across more than 30 countries on six continents. Customers and partners can access the São Paulo lab through their Digital Realty account manager. The announcement was distributed through GlobeNewswire and republished by The Manila Times.

stories.Headline: What Are You Telling AI? Simple Ways to Protect Your Privacy
stories.Summary:
The Baltimore Times published an article on November 7, 2026, by Karen Clay, titled "What Are You Telling AI? Simple Ways to Protect Your Privacy." It describes how the everyday use of AI assistants has grown quickly since 2022, with people using them for medical bills, résumés, and personal conversations. The author raises the question of what happens to information after it is sent, noting that it may be stored, reviewed by people, or used to improve models. The piece defines an "AI footprint" as the trail left through conversations, uploaded files, pictures, recordings, and connected accounts.

The article offers practical steps for users. It advises leaving out identifiers such as Social Security numbers, account numbers, and full birth dates, and suggests replacing names with labels and removing identifying details from uploaded documents. It recommends checking data control and model-improvement settings before starting a conversation, and notes that OpenAI says temporary chats are not used for training but may be kept for up to 30 days for safety. Google, according to the piece, keeps Gemini temporary chats for 72 hours. Users are also urged to delete old chats and saved memories, since deleting one does not necessarily remove the other, and to review device permissions and connected accounts.

A second article, from usmagazine.com dated November 5, 2026, examines privacy concerns around virtual try-on tools used for cosmetics, eyewear, and apparel. It explains that Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act requires written consent before a company collects biometric data such as facial scans. A class action against MAC Cosmetics alleges its try-on tool scanned facial geometry without that consent, and the company's motion to dismiss was denied in June 2026, leaving the case open. A 2024 suit against Estée Lauder was dismissed because the plaintiff could not show the company could identify customers from the scans.

The same article describes the EU General Data Protection Regulation, in force since 2018, which requires that data processing be lawful, fair, and transparent, limited to disclosed purposes, kept accurate, and held only as long as necessary. The company acting as data controller must be able to prove compliance. The article also points readers to the published policies of ChatGPT and Google for information on how their try-on photos are handled. Both articles frame the issue as one where the rules are still developing, leaving consumers to check policies and settings for themselves.

stories.Headline: The AI Trade Unwind Crushed The S&P 500 This Week
stories.Summary:
Markets slid sharply in the first week of November 2026 as a sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks spread across the United States and Asia. According to the Mott Capital Management analysis, the SMH semiconductor fund fell more than 11% over the week, the Nasdaq nearly 5%, the S&P 500 nearly 3%, and the IWM about 2%. The market had rallied on Wednesday after the midterm elections, with the S&P 500 up about 1.58%, but it gave those gains back on Thursday as semiconductor shares continued to fall and correlations among stocks rose. Business Insider reported that the Nasdaq 100 entered an official correction on Thursday, and that Asian tech shares were hit hard on Friday, when South Korea's Kospi fell 9% in early trading, triggering a trading halt, and Japan's Nikkei 225 sank 7%.

The Mott analysis describes a volatility unwind that masked weakness beneath the surface. The 1-day VIX had risen to about 23 before the election, implying a move of roughly 1.4% for Wednesday, and once that event passed, options premiums decayed and hedges came off, lifting the index while technology shares fell. By Thursday's close the 1-day VIX stood at 36.8, and the author expects limited room for volatility to fall further, noting that the one-month implied correlation of 20 is high relative to recent months but low historically. The analysis flags CPI due Tuesday, November 10, and PPI after it as near-term catalysts, and it says the S&P 500 sits on an important support level that a break could push lower. Business Insider adds that investors fear Democratic election wins could bring tighter regulation of data centers and AI development, which could threaten the spending boom behind the rally.

Michael Kramer, a member and investment adviser representative with Mott Capital Management, wrote the Mott analysis, which presents his own views and is published for informational purposes only. He argued that the market could keep unwinding if Nvidia, Micron, and Broadcom stop working, and he said Thursday and Friday might prove to be an isolated event. Business Insider quotes Charu Chanana, Saxo's chief investment strategist, who said the sharp correction partly reflects a reassessment of future US infrastructure demand and crowded investor positioning in AI beneficiaries. She said the market is repricing future expectations rather than reacting to a sudden collapse in current demand, and that it may be the end of rewarding every company linked to AI equally.

Looking ahead, the sources point to the inflation data due next week and to the question of whether AI spending will pay off. Business Insider reports that investors increasingly want evidence of returns and may favor firms with strong finances and established customers over those relying on outside funding. Chanana described the sell-off as possibly not the end of the AI trade, while Kramer's analysis warned that mechanical unwinding could continue and that caution is warranted. stories.Headline: Kids Hooked on AI Chatbots Are Showing Dramatically Worse Mental Health
stories.Summary:
A new survey from the mental health advocacy group JED Foundation has found that heavy use of AI chatbots among children is tied to worse mental health. Futurism reported on the findings on November 5, 2026, and NaturalNews.com summarized the report the following day. According to the survey, 90 percent of children aged nine to 17 have used an AI chatbot. The majority, 58 percent, use one for schoolwork, and 57 percent said they also turn to AI when feeling sad, stressed, lonely or overwhelmed.

The survey found that the use goes beyond coping. Twelve percent of students said they use AI for friendship or companionship, and a separate survey from last year found that nearly one in five high schoolers said they or a friend had used AI for a romantic relationship. Young people who turn to AI while in emotional distress were more likely to report poor mental health and well-being, along with a greater history of suicidal thoughts and attempts. A 15-year-old in Texas, Arjun Sharda, told Oregon Public Broadcasting he kept asking ChatGPT whether he would be okay after fearing he would fail an early chemistry test.

Kayla Anderson, a psychologist and the JED Foundation's vice president of research and evaluation, said the data allowed researchers to compare how young people use AI with indicators of well-being and suicidal history. She cautioned that the evidence does not establish causation. In her words, it is unclear whether AI use contributes to poor mental health or whether students already in distress are more likely to turn to it. Anne Maheux, a developmental psychologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who was not involved in the work, pointed to other research suggesting both may be true. She said kids with worse mental health seek out AI for help, but that the use may make those struggles worse.

The findings come amid a wave of government action. NaturalNews.com reported that California Governor Gavin Newsom signed 13 bills on September 15, 2026, to regulate minors' access to social media and AI chatbots, including limits on addictive features for users under 16. New York's law, signed by Governor Kathy Hochul, bans unsafe AI companion features for minors and takes effect January 1, 2027. New York City also moved in early September to bar student AI use in public schools through eighth grade. Florida has sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging the company hid serious risks of ChatGPT, particularly for children, and NaturalNews.com says ChatGPT faces at least eight lawsuits alleging it worsened users' mental health.

stories.Headline: IREN Says New AI Cloud Customers Are Prepaying 90% of the Chips
stories.Summary:
IREN, the AI cloud operator, said on November 5, 2026 that a new customer will prepay most of the cost of the graphics processors that will serve it. After the quarter ended, IREN signed a five-year AI Cloud contract at about $22 million of annualized revenue per megawatt of IT load. The customer is prepaying about 90% of the related GPU capital spending. The announcement came as the company's shares fell sharply in the regular session, closing at $18.03, down 16.95%, before recovering to $19.95 after hours.

The prepayments could ease IREN's funding needs, since customer money covers much of the hardware that would otherwise require outside financing. Even so, IREN's cash fell to $3.52 billion from $5.90 billion, and its net debt rose to $4.43 billion from $216 million. The company also signed a short-term contract at more than $40 million per megawatt, expanded a deal with a leading frontier AI lab, and signed new contracts for older H100 GPUs at double the earlier pricing. IREN did not name the five-year customer, and it gave no megawatt counts, GPU numbers, total contract value or start dates.

Chief Financial Officer Anthony Lewis said some recent contracts carry prepayments of up to 90% and that IREN targets total GPU financing of 90% of related capex, including prepayments. Co-CEO Daniel Roberts said lower-credit customers tend to make larger prepayments, which complicates the positive reading of the deals. Chief Commercial Officer Kent Draper said the company does not comment on individual contracts. Lewis also said two-thirds of the $20.3 billion backlog, which grew 22%, comes from investment-grade customers including Microsoft and NVIDIA.

The company's target of more than $4 billion in operating annual recurring revenue is now set for January 31, 2027 instead of year-end 2026, and it could slip to the end of February 2027. Roberts said Microsoft asked IREN to rework the network at its 200 MW Horizon 1 site, which he described as a negligible extra capital cost. IREN plans $15 billion of capital spending for the rest of fiscal 2027, of which $9 billion is covered by cash and committed funding, while $6 billion depends on market conditions. Investors are watching whether the capacity target is met and whether the remaining gap is covered mainly by new stock.

stories.Headline: Teaching AI to build scientific models
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Anthropic published a guest post on November 6, 2026, written by Jakob Macke, Daniel Gedon, and Stefan Wahl of the ELLIS Institute Tübingen and the University of Tübingen, about how AI is beginning to change scientific modeling. They recalled that in 1951 the Cambridge computer was out of action for six months, which left Andrew Huxley to solve the equations he and Alan Hodgkin had written for how a squid nerve cell fires by hand, a process that took him over three weeks. The authors use this episode to argue that a model is only useful if it yields understanding, not just a fit to data. Their point is that many different models can reproduce the same measurements, so a scientist needs to know which features make a model work and which set it apart from failures. The post breaks scientific modeling into three steps: building the model, constraining it by tuning its parameters to real measurements, and interpreting what it says about the real system.

Constraining is the step where AI has advanced most, and the authors describe simulation-based inference, a method that runs a simulator many times, for example about 100,000 times for a model like Hodgkin-Huxley, and trains a neural network to return the range of parameters that could have produced a given output. Once trained, that network can analyze new data in seconds, a speed that let researchers point telescopes at colliding neutron stars while the signal was still detectable. The authors also note that the same method has been applied to nerve cell models, where it shows which parameters the data pins down and where another experiment is needed. The authors describe the building step as now partly handled by AI as well, with LLM-based agents writing candidate model code, running it, comparing it to data, and revising until the fit is good enough. They say several such systems have appeared in the past two years, and that until recently designing the model itself was thought to be something only humans could do.

They caution that a model that replicates data does not by that fact provide insight, since different models can explain the same data equally well. An agent that returns only one of those models, they argue, hides the rest, in the same way a single best-fit set of numbers does. The post places this work in the longer history of the Hodgkin-Huxley model, which remains the standard description of electrical activity in neurons more than 70 years later. The authors note that Hodgkin and Huxley shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and that a later team found a related potassium channel protein with four identical pieces, matching the fourth power the original model had required. The article does not describe a specific next step beyond the continued development of these methods, so it leaves open how far AI agents will take over the building and interpreting of models.

stories.Headline: GitLab 19.5 integrates agentic development, enhances AI governance
stories.Summary:
GitLab released version 19.5 of its DevOps platform on October 15, building agentic software development and governance directly into the product. The headline change is that the GitLab Model Context Protocol server is now generally available. That lets compatible tools such as Claude Code and Cursor reach GitLab's wider tool catalogue and call GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and flows. A separate announcement reported on November 5 added capabilities for workflow automation, supply chain security, credential management and AI cost monitoring, aimed at helping organisations govern AI-generated code as it moves from development to production. GitLab said active users of agentic development on its platform grew 200% year over year over the last three months.

The release adds several controls for external agents. Security teams can see which agents are in use, by whom and against which projects, and administrators can choose which MCP toolsets are exposed, a simple form of least-privilege design. On GitLab.com, MCP rate limits are 60 requests per minute for Free users and 600 for Premium and Ultimate users, with reconnects and retries counted. Externally connected agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can be brought into AI governance through the GitLab CLI, with qualifying sessions recorded by user, agent, project and timing, and audit events can be streamed to a SIEM system. The Duo CLI also gains an auto mode, off by default and controllable at instance, group and project levels, which lets agents run tools without approval for each command, while anything marked "Always Deny" stays blocked.

GitLab Secrets Manager, built on OpenBao, is now generally available, uses existing group and project permissions, scopes secrets to the jobs that need them and generates audit events. GitLab says it can save up to 50% compared with hosting a separate vault, and it is due on GitLab Self-Managed with the 19.5 release. GitLab Artifact Central is in beta on GitLab.com, with Self-Managed availability planned for later this month, and the company claims it can cut total cost of ownership by up to 50% against alternative tooling. GitLab Dependency Firewall, in early access, checks packages against organisational policies on age, vulnerability severity, malicious package detection and licence compliance before they enter a build. The /goal command is also generally available, letting developers describe an objective and have GitLab Duo hand implementation and verification to a governed flow.

All of these claims and figures come from GitLab itself, as reported by TechGig and ET CIO, and the company says the changes connect development stages through shared workflows, policies and audit records. It argues that organisations often use separate tools for coding, issue tracking, CI/CD, security, artifact management and deployment, which makes consistent identity and policy controls hard to maintain. The company also reported that over the same three months secure repositories grew 100%, user namespaces rose 80% and CI/CD pipelines grew 40%. It is expanding security configuration profiles too, so organisations can centrally set excluded paths, analyser images and full-history scans for Secret Detection and SAST.

The release arrives as the wider conversation about agentic AI shifts toward governance. A CIO.com piece sponsored by HCLTech cited a survey in which 87% of participating enterprises use generative or agentic AI in IT operations, and research from Omdia in which respondents expect about 43% of major AI initiatives to fail. It argued that governance should be built in from the outset, with human oversight kept for high-stakes decisions. The ET CIO article said GitLab also plans to make Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 and 5.1 available, though the text provided cuts off before further details.

stories.Headline: Who Owns DeepSeek, The Chinese AI Company?
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek, a Chinese AI lab, drew global attention when it launched its R1 model in 2025, using a mixture of experts design to generate responses at a far lower cost than rivals. The app quickly grew popular, and the launch set off a global technology stock selloff that year. The company has since released its V4-Flash model, which the articles say is more than 90% cheaper to run than peer models such as Kimi K3, GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5. Its models are subject to censorship under Chinese law, which may limit future growth.

The company was founded by Liang Wenfeng, an electronics engineer from Zhejiang University, who funded its launch in 2023 with profits from his hedge fund, High-Flyer. In DeepSeek's second funding round it raised about $15 billion from backers including Tencent Holdings and CATL, and the articles say 27% of that funding is state-owned, with the China National AI Industry Investment Fund contributing about $150 million. Liang is one of four Chinese tech entrepreneurs the media have dubbed China's "fantastic four," and the company is reportedly considering an IPO on Shanghai's STAR Market. The market reaction to R1 was severe: NVIDIA lost $589 billion in market value in a single day, the largest single-day loss in the history of the U.S. stock market.

The articles tie DeepSeek's efficiency to its technical methods, including its mixture of experts architecture, which activates only the parts of a model needed for a task, along with optimization for cheaper GPUs, model distillation and reinforcement learning. Before U.S. export controls took effect in 2022, High-Flyer and other Chinese entities stockpiled NVIDIA GPUs, which DeepSeek later used. The U.S. has tried to limit China's access to such chips, and China has responded by advancing its homegrown chip manufacturing to reduce reliance on Western chips and tools. The articles suggest the wider AI industry could learn from these efficiency gains to ease the heavy resource demands of data centers.

stories.Headline: Angelo State Launches Two-Year AI Center of Excellence Initiative
stories.Summary:
Angelo State University in San Angelo, Texas, has selected Kovexa Solutions LLC to advance its Artificial Intelligence Center of Excellence through a two-year initiative announced on November 6, 2026. The initiative is meant to equip students, faculty and community members to apply AI responsibly to challenges facing the region. Both the university and San Angelo LIVE! reported the partnership on the same day. The announcement made clear that the work is intended to be practical rather than theoretical.

The initiative organizes its work around five core pillars called Govern, Learn, Scale, Build and Connect. A two-year study will track its impact and how responsibly the technology is being used. The university says the program is designed so that people across campus and the surrounding community can take part. Officials describe the effort as a way to prepare the workforce for what comes next. The structure gives participants a framework for moving from ideas to measurable results.

Dr. Scarlet Clouse, dean of Angelo State's College of Education and director of the Kay Bailey Hutchison Institute, said the goal is to foster responsible AI use among faculty, staff, students and the community. She said that when students work with faculty and community partners on real problems, they build practical skills and learn both what the technology can and cannot do. Andrew Ko, founder of Kovexa Solutions, said the best starting point is a problem worth solving. He said his firm is helping the university connect the right people with the right technologies to produce practical outcomes.

Kovexa Solutions describes itself as an education-focused consultancy that helps leaders turn AI into scalable strategies, custom applications and measurable outcomes. Under the partnership, the firm provides strategic guidance and a technical framework meant to help institutions and regional leaders adopt AI responsibly. Further information is available at kovexa.com. Questions about the initiative may be directed to Dr. Clouse at the university.

stories.Headline: IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge pair a 120-qubit Nighthawk with an AMD supercomputer to test quantum error correction
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, IBM, AMD and the Department of Energy-funded Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory unveiled a joint platform for quantum error correction that links a quantum processor with a classical supercomputer. The setup places IBM's 120-qubit Quantum Nighthawk processor alongside ORNL's Umbra system, which runs AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen EPYC CPUs. The platform will also connect to the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility. Reporters covering the launch noted that the partners aim to bring more classical computing into the work to speed progress.

The project supports the Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission, which targets 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028. IBM says it has run experiments with up to 70 logical qubits and 438 hard operations, so the partners would need roughly a 230-fold rise in hard-operation count to reach the goal. Researchers will compare what each error-correction technique requires in qubits, time, samples and classical resources. They will also test concatenated and space-time codes, algorithm-aware decoders and hardware-aware compilation through IBM's Quantum System API. Today's qubits err roughly once every few hundred operations, while algorithms such as Shor's need billions of error-free operations.

IBM, AMD and ORNL are the organizations behind the platform, and their leaders described its purpose in their own terms. Jay Gambetta, director of IBM Research, said the question is no longer whether error correction will work on quantum hardware. AMD executive vice president Mark Papermaster described the platform as an important step toward scalable, efficient infrastructure for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Travis Humble, director of the Quantum Science Center at ORNL, said solving error-correction challenges is a laboratory priority. IBM also said the results may shape its planned Quantum Starling, its first fault-tolerant machine.

The platform builds on earlier collaborations among the same partners. In 2025, IBM and AMD demonstrated an algorithm that decodes quantum errors efficiently on AMD chips. Earlier in 2026, IBM and ORNL used quantum computers and the Frontier supercomputer to simulate magnetic materials and fusion-fuel candidates. Other companies are pursuing similar goals, with Quantinuum expecting its Nexus system to automate error correction through 2029. The articles do not say when the partners expect the first results from the new platform.

stories.Headline: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling despite usage increase
stories.Summary:
Ramp, the spending platform, released data showing that companies are using more AI tools but their spending on them has stalled, flattening out over late summer even as token volumes rose. Token spend grew only 1.5 percent across August and September, after growing 42 percent from June to July. The report's lead economist, Ara Kharazian, told TechCrunch that almost all AI spending comes from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies. He added that a slowdown among the top 1 percent of firms was enough to pull overall revenue down, even with volumes still climbing.

The top 1 percent of firms, which Kharazian described as the most heavily invested in AI, spent just under $10,000 per employee in August and September, below their summer peaks. Median firms spend $12 to $15 per employee each month, while the top 10 percent spend $600 to $1,000. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for its GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. Anthropic also reduced prices for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, a move the company said in a recent filing cut its revenue growth by about $600 million. October showed an 8.9 percent rebound in token spend from September to October, though Kharazian said the headwinds remain strong.

Kharazian attributed the slowdown mainly to competition rather than weak demand, pointing to price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic, enterprise offerings from Meta and Nvidia, and cheaper open-source models from China and the United States. He also noted that companies are getting better at controlling AI costs by using default settings that avoid expensive models, setting employee budgets, and routing tasks to cheaper models. Bloomberg reported that Anthropic's potential valuation fell from $2 trillion in early October to between $1.2 trillion and $1.3 trillion, and that OpenAI lowered its proposed valuation from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion. Both companies have also reportedly cut their fundraising goals.

Investors have assumed that new AI uses, such as personal agents, will sustain rapid growth in spending, much as AI coding did. Kharazian is skeptical, saying that personal agents are not as economically productive as coding and may not drive the same level of spending. He said the data suggests the era of hypergrowth in AI spending may be over. The report comes as Anthropic nears an IPO, which raises questions about how investors will view the company's revenue trajectory.

stories.Headline: Employed job seekers are shunning companies which use AI interviews — and I don't blame them
stories.Summary:
Employed job seekers are increasingly turning down companies that use AI-run job interviews, and one TechRadar article says the writer understands why. Candidates who already have jobs are reportedly avoiding employers that screen applicants with AI interviewers, a shift the article ties to growing unease about the technology in hiring. The piece sits within a wider run of coverage on how AI is reshaping the job market, including how interviews now work. The article's author says he does not blame those who refuse, and the sources available here do not give a specific number for how many candidates are declining.

Separately, CNBC reported on November 5, 2026, that job seekers should expect questions about AI in interviews, even for roles that are not technical. The article draws on a September 2026 survey of more than 1,500 U.S. workers by the job board ZipRecruiter, which found that 82.5% of workers use AI to some degree at work while only 62.8% had received AI training from their employer. Non-technical job posts mentioning AI rose to 4.3% of all posts on ZipRecruiter at the time of the report, up from 1.9% in 2025. Lisa Dubler, director of career services at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, says candidates should be ready to discuss how they use AI, how they might use it in a given role, and how they think about its safety and ethics. ZipRecruiter labor economist Nicole Bachaud adds that only about 10% of workers list AI skills prominently on their résumés, even though employers are very interested in them.

The CNBC piece offers advice for candidates facing these questions. Dubler tells job seekers to always be honest, to use examples from past projects, and to explain how AI supported their work and how those skills carry over to the new role. Career coach Freda Thomas suggests asking clarifying questions when an AI question feels too broad, and recommends that candidates use the interview to check whether a company's values and AI policies match their own. The article also points to free resources, such as AI courses on LinkedIn Learning and YouTube, for candidates who lack hands-on experience with the technology. Workers are divided on the matter, the survey found: 52.6% said AI has made their job more enjoyable, while about a quarter said they want to leave their job because of AI-related concerns.

stories.Headline: India flags Chinese-linked AI tools in hacking campaign against financial firms - CNA
stories.Summary:
India's cybersecurity agency, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), issued an advisory on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, naming a hacking group it calls "Crafty Falcon" as the source of a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial firms. The group has breached non-bank lenders, fintech firms and cryptocurrency exchanges. CERT-In said the attackers use publicly available AI tools to automate break-ins "at machine speed" and described the threat as active and ongoing. The advisory came after a series of cyberattacks on Indian banks and non-bank lenders in recent weeks.

The agency named four tools the group uses: ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn and CyberStrikeAI, of which security researchers have linked at least two to China. According to cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike, China-made ARTEX has been used against South Korean banks since late September, and a China-linked group used it in an espionage campaign against more than 200 organisations in at least 14 countries. The advisory itself does not say the attacks were state-sponsored, and the tools are freely available online, though ARTEX was made private by its developer last month after its link to the South Korean attacks. CERT-In did not name the affected companies or say how much money was stolen.

CERT-In said Crafty Falcon surveys its targets with machine intelligence and moves money by invoking victims' own payment and disbursement systems. The attackers time their operations around holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring periods to delay detection, and they struck again at firms whose fixes after earlier alerts were incomplete. Reuters, citing a police complaint, reported that two Mumbai-based non-bank lenders lost about $2 million through more than 700 unauthorised instant transfers from ICICI Bank accounts on October 8 and 9. The complaint said hackers compromised application programming interfaces, the software links banks use to send loan-disbursal instructions to non-bank lenders and fintech firms. CERT-In, the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre and the IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment, and CERT-In did not say which incidents were linked to Crafty Falcon.

The wider context includes several other recent incidents. State Bank of India, the country's largest lender, disclosed a dark-web leak of 3,897 customer records last month. Spandana Sphoorty Financial, a non-bank lender, reported unauthorised debits from a bank account on November 1, and AU Small Finance Bank said it was probing a potential customer-data leak. The Reserve Bank of India has tightened cybersecurity checks in response to the spate of attacks. The articles do not say what further steps authorities will take.

stories.Headline: Parents sue Google after discovering what daughter was doing with AI on school Chromebook
stories.Summary:
The parents of a 13-year-old girl identified as Emma filed a lawsuit against Google on Monday 2 November in a court in California. They allege that she used Google's AI technology on a school-issued Chromebook to plan a possible suicide and her funeral. The case is believed to be the first to accuse Google of negligence over AI-powered search features reached through a school laptop. Another report describes the 104-page complaint as coming from parents in North Carolina, and says it centers on the Gemini chatbot.

According to the complaint, Emma could not open Google's Gemini app or OpenAI's ChatGPT at school, since both had been blocked, but she could still use Google's search engine and its AI features. The family says she had no history of mental illness, yet within months of using the search tools she fell into what the filing calls a quiet spiral into a severe psychological crisis. The other report says that as her chats grew more frequent through January and February 2026, the AI convinced her she had major psychological disorders and that suicide was the only escape. On 17 March, the school's monitoring software flagged a document titled "Funeral" and alerted her parents. Her mother then found her writing a farewell letter, and her father stepped in.

Andrew Liddell, one of the family's attorneys, told AFP on Thursday 5 November that schools should switch off search until Google removes AI mode from search or can ensure every student is safe while using AI. Google says its AI Mode has safeguards against self-harm and works to stop people from bypassing them. Company spokesperson Jose Castaneda told AFP that Google is reviewing the claims and takes them very seriously. The articles do not report any ruling or response in court.

The suit adds to growing legal pressure on technology companies over harms to young people. OpenAI faces several wrongful death lawsuits, including one from the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, who died by suicide after allegedly getting harmful advice from ChatGPT. In January, Google and Character.AI agreed to settle several lawsuits brought by families of teenagers out of court. Meta was recently ordered to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found it liable for deceiving users about privacy and content moderation. Separately, Google, TikTok and Meta sued California on Wednesday to block a law, signed by Governor Gavin Newsom in September, that bans addictive social media features for users under 16 and is due to take effect on 1 January 2027.

stories.Headline: 3 Great AI Stocks To Own In November 2026
stories.Summary:
The announcement named in the headline's lead item is a Simply Wall St shortlist of three US AI stocks, published on 7 November 2026, with Marvell Technology as the first company covered. The piece was written by Bailey Pemberton and framed against a strong US jobs report that showed 165,000 new roles added and unemployment falling. It presents the three chipmakers as companies expected to grow earnings quickly while keeping their finances in decent shape. Marvell is described as a designer and seller of data-center chips, mainly Ethernet and storage controllers that help large cloud operators move and store data.

On the numbers, the article puts Marvell's revenue at about US$9.5b, earned from designing, developing and selling integrated circuits to customers across China, Taiwan, the United States and other regions. It says the company's networking and storage chips are tightly tied to the AI and cloud workloads that analysts expect to drive strong earnings over the next few years. The article also quotes management guidance that the optical interconnect business should grow more than 50% year on year in fiscal 2027, well ahead of a guide of more than 20% for the ASIC segment. That optical growth is linked to 800G and 1.6T DSP adoption, CXL switch attach rates and an eventual ramp of Photonic Fabric products.

Responsibility for the piece lies with Simply Wall St, which says the article is general in nature and was produced with the help of AI automation. The firm states that its commentary rests on historical data and analyst forecasts using what it calls an unbiased method, and that it is not financial advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any stock. stories.Headline: Saudi Arabia introduces AI principles for media
stories.Summary:
Saudi Arabia has introduced a national framework that governs how artificial intelligence may be used in media, setting out principles meant to promote transparency, accuracy and accountability. The AI Principles in Media document, reported by the Saudi Press Agency, asks media practitioners and content creators to say when material has been generated or assisted by AI. They are asked to use clear labels, watermarks or metadata so audiences can tell synthetic content from authentic records. The move follows growing use of AI tools to produce text, images, video and audio. Officials cite concerns about misinformation, intellectual property rights and user privacy.

The guidelines lay out eight core principles that cover transparency and disclosure, factual accuracy and credibility, privacy and the protection of public figures, and the prevention of misleading content. They also address accountability across the full life of a piece of content, impartiality and integrity, public awareness and empowerment, and ongoing impact assessment with regulatory compliance. The framework cautions against treating generative AI as an authoritative source of information. It stresses that human verification, deepfake detection and awareness of possible algorithmic bias are needed. Taken together, these points set expectations for how newsrooms and creators should check and label their work.

The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, known as SDAIA, worked with the General Authority of Media Regulation to promote responsible use of the technology. The two bodies organized the AI for Impact forum, which brought together more than 250 media professionals, digital influencers and content creators. Participants discussed ethical standards and practical risks at each stage of production, from research and scriptwriting to editing, audience analytics and impact assessment. The forum also marked the launch of the Impact Creators program, which will offer theoretical instruction and practical training in content verification and professional production standards. According to the reports, the program aims to help Saudi creators use AI safely and effectively while strengthening trust in the Kingdom's digital media sector.

stories.Headline: Korea Targets 60,000 AI Workers for Small Firms by 2030
stories.Summary:
The Korea SMEs and Startups Agency, known as KOSME, opened a manufacturing AI training center at its Small and Venture Business Training Institute in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province, with the aim of training 60,000 AI specialists for small and venture businesses by 2030. The center pairs AI technology with existing training facilities and includes a learning space, a vision practice lab, an AX experience zone and an integrated control room showroom. It will run on a trial basis through the end of this year before offering regular courses next year. Separately, the Pakistani government said it aims to develop one million AI professionals by 2030 under its National AI Policy, a goal announced by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal at a Pakistan-Russia IT collaboration forum in Islamabad.

The Korean agency's plan centers on three directions: training specialists to lead AI transformation, strengthening job skills tied to real field work, and expanding the public sector's role in balanced regional development. Officials expect hiring competitiveness at small businesses to rise as a result, especially for job seekers who hold AI skills. In Pakistan, Iqbal said the country produces more than 75,000 graduates a year and will build seven new AI centers to link research, skills training, startups and industry. He also described e-Pakistan as one of five core pillars of the National Economic Transformation Plan, which aims to make the country a trillion-dollar economy by 2035.

Korean lawmakers also discussed related youth policy, with Rep. Yoon Sang-hyun of the People Power Party holding a National Assembly forum on a proposed youth income deduction. The design would give wage and business income earners aged 19 to 34 an annual deduction of 3 million won for five years, phased down for those with reference income above 50 million won and unavailable to those earning 70 million won or more. A 300,000 won annual tax credit was offered as a comparison option. Supporters argue that easing the tax burden in early working years would raise job seekers' real disposable income. Iqbal, for his part, said success should be judged by the trade, investment and employment that cooperation with Russia generates rather than by announcements, and he pointed to automation, cloud computing, cybersecurity and digital platforms as areas for joint work.

stories.Headline: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is reportedly improving its AI systems about twice as fast as it did a year ago, according to an independent analysis released on November 5, 2026, by Model Evaluation and Threat Research, a Berkeley-based nonprofit known as METR. The group reviewed Anthropic's internal data over roughly eleven weeks, from mid-August through late October, and interviewed staff, a level of access the group described as unprecedented. Its estimate covers the company's progress on well-specified tasks, and METR said it believes much of the speed-up comes from the company's own AI systems helping with research. The analysis was released as Anthropic prepares for a public stock offering later this month.

The findings matter because Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, in its July 2026 version, defines a threshold for "dramatically accelerated progress due to AI," and the analysis suggests that threshold may already have been crossed. Under the policy, the test is whether progress runs at double the rate of the fastest sustained pace seen before AI contributed much to research, and whether that doubling is plausibly due to AI automating research. The author of a companion commentary, Ajeya Cotra, noted that the report's redacted evidence was the majority of what the researchers found most informative. She also estimated that for progress to double overall, researcher productivity would have to rise several times over, perhaps around ten times, which she said lines up with informal self-reports from Anthropic staff.

Responsibility for the analysis lies with METR's researchers, who said the redactions limited how precisely they could describe the acceleration and that their team did not fully agree on every estimate. Anthropic has not publicly responded to requests for comment on the report. METR stated that it could be overstating its findings, since the speed-up might apply only to tasks that can be graded automatically rather than messier work, and it also noted that Anthropic's earlier progress figures might have been understated. METR said it could confidently rule out growth in training computing power as the main cause. The commentary also argues that if the trend continues, it could compound rapidly and that current safeguards are far from adequate for such a pace.

The broader context is a policy debate about whether AI development should slow down. Dario Amodei, Anthropic's chief executive, called on September 12 for the industry to slow the pace of capability improvements so that safety measures could keep up, and the METR analysis suggests the company's work has continued to accelerate in the meantime. The report's authors and outside commentators say more transparency about the underlying evidence is needed, since external scientists currently cannot check the data behind the conclusions. What happens next depends on how the company responds, what regulators and the public make of the redacted material, and whether independent researchers are given the chance to examine the evidence themselves.

stories.Headline: Nvidia H200 Chips Pile Up in Hong Kong as China Holds Back Import Approvals
stories.Summary:
Around 600,000 Nvidia H200 AI chips are reportedly sitting in warehouses in Hong Kong, waiting to be shipped to mainland China. Reuters and other foreign media reported this on November 5, local time, and BusinessKorea published its article on November 6, 2026. The stockpile is held up because Chinese authorities have not approved large-scale imports, even though the U.S. government has partly eased its export restrictions on China. Chinese authorities have allowed only limited imports for selected companies so far.

Based on publicly listed prices, the inventory is estimated at between $20 billion and $30 billion, roughly 29 trillion to 44 trillion won. The reports say this is the first time the size of the stockpile has been disclosed publicly. Alibaba and ByteDance have reportedly secured only about 10,000 H200 units each, which falls well short of their needs. Some chips have reached China through intermediaries, and prices in the country's informal market have risen sharply. In late October, the gray-market price for a server with eight H200 chips exceeded 6 million yuan, about 1.3 billion won or $900,088, roughly three times the level a year earlier.

China's position is widely read as an effort to protect its domestic chip industry and reduce its reliance on U.S. technology. According to the article, Beijing appears to favor companies such as Huawei, allowing Nvidia chips for training AI models while encouraging Chinese-made chips for running models in live services. The H200 is considered more powerful than domestic alternatives and works with Nvidia's software ecosystem, which makes it attractive for training large AI models. Reuters reported that Chinese authorities first communicated restrictions in mid-January, then shifted to conditional purchases by selected firms, with more than 400,000 units reportedly approved for Alibaba, ByteDance and Tencent. Some of those approvals have not produced orders because the conditions remain unclear.

The article also notes that the United States has restricted advanced AI chip exports to China since 2022, then eased some limits after 2025 trade talks, allowing H200 sales to approved customers. Chinese customs authorities have reportedly told some companies to hold off on purchases, which could delay deliveries further. Separately, ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have reportedly placed orders for more than 3 million RTX Pro 5500 graphics cards, worth over $35 billion at list prices, which are distinct from the stranded H200 inventory. The article does not say how the standoff will be resolved.

stories.Headline: AI stocks in my ISA are tanking. Here’s what I’m doing now
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, 5 November 2026, AI stocks sold off sharply on Wall Street after Democrats' election wins raised fears that data center construction could slow. According to the Dallas Express, the Nasdaq Composite closed down 5.5%, the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1,833 points, or 3.4%. Nvidia shares dropped 9.3%, Advanced Micro Devices fell 17.3%, and CoreWeave lost 9.8%. Investors were worried that incoming officials could delay the AI infrastructure buildout, and financing costs and doubts about AI valuations had already weighed on the sector. The main policy at the center of the concern is a proposal from Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who defeated Governor Greg Abbott in Texas.

Her campaign platform calls for a moratorium on new data centers until lawmakers enact new rules. Her July 23 priorities also ask data center operators to hire licensed union labor, stop relying on subsidies, and show their projects will not raise household electricity or water costs. She also proposes more local input, limits on nondisclosure agreements, and rules making water contracts unenforceable if they threaten a community's supply. In a November 1 interview, Hinojosa described the pause as applying to new permits rather than projects already under construction. These remain policy proposals rather than enacted law.

Elon Musk shared a post from investor Gavin Baker on Thursday with the single word "Interesting," without endorsing any specific proposal. Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer of Atreides Management, argued that Hinojosa's approach would let already permitted projects finish, which he said covers all of 2027 and likely much of 2028. He placed newly permitted projects subject to future rules on a 2028 or 2029 timeline. The Dallas Express notes that this schedule reflects Baker's own assessment, since Hinojosa's written platform does not establish it. Separately, Governor Abbott had already directed Texas regulators on August 3 to audit data centers moving through the grid-connection process before approving more projects, and the state's grid operator plans to publish a report on or before December 10.

Meanwhile, the Independent UK Finance, as reported by Yahoo UK, described AI firms as hit in the worst stock market crash for 18 months, and a separate Yahoo UK column by Edward Sheldon describes falling AI holdings in his ISA and SIPP. Sheldon says he is not panicking, takes a long-term view, and sees opportunities, particularly in Micron, which he says has fallen from about $1,090 to $720 over roughly a month. He cites analyst forecasts of $174 in earnings per share for the year ending 31 August 2027 and a forward price-to-earnings ratio of about four, while noting memory demand is highly cyclical. The articles present Sheldon's views as his own, and he discloses that he owns shares in several of the companies mentioned.

stories.Headline: Kakao Unveils AI Model for Text and Image-Based Decision-Making
stories.Summary:
Kakao has released an artificial intelligence model called Kanana-2-v-decide that analyzes text and images to make classifications and choices rather than writing sentence-based replies. The company published the model on Hugging Face on November 6, 2026, after building it in-house on top of its multimodal model Kanana-2-v-3b, which accepts both text and image inputs. Instead of generating prose, the model returns probabilities, selections, or scores that developers can route into their own workflows. Kakao plans to first use it in internal projects covering web search and automated product category classification.

The model offers three kinds of output, and developers pick the one that fits their service. It can estimate the probability that a stated condition is true, assign probabilities across several options to identify the best fit, or produce scores reflecting how likely each evaluation level is. As an example, a customer who sends a photo of a damaged product with a replacement request could have the image and message analyzed together to confirm the damage, classify the inquiry, and gauge the customer's emotional state. Predefined rules can then send the customer to the right support channel or supply replacement instructions.

Kakao also uses an embedding design that turns inputs and candidate options into numerical vectors and compares their similarity, so stored vectors can be reused for repeated requests. In tests on a single Nvidia H200 GPU, the company reported an average response time below 0.04 seconds. The model is released under the Kanana Open License, which allows both research and commercial use. Kakao is the company responsible for the model, and it described the release as an effort to improve its own performance across the internal projects it has named.

The Elec, which reported the launch, notes that Kakao intends to later combine search and decision-making into a single model. A separate industry piece published around the same time argues that supply chain planning must shift from periodic forecasting toward continuous decisioning and probabilistic models that treat demand and supply as ranges. That piece also warns that AI systems amplify the quality of the logic beneath them, so flawed assumptions can lead to faster bad decisions. Taken together, the two articles suggest that AI decision tools are moving from experimental research into routine operational use across different industries.

stories.Headline: UPDATE - RJ Lee Group and Carahsoft Partner to Bring Post-Quantum Data Protection and Phishing-Resistant Authentication Solutions to the Public Sector
stories.Summary:
On November 5, 2026, RJ Lee Group, a Monroeville, Pennsylvania scientific and technical firm, and Carahsoft Technology Corp., a Reston, Virginia government IT provider, announced a partnership to bring RJ Lee's quantum-resilient cybersecurity products to public sector buyers. Under the agreement, Carahsoft will act as RJ Lee's Master Government Aggregator, making the products available through Carahsoft's reseller partners and its NASA SEWP V and E&I Cooperative Services contracts. A later version of the same announcement, dated November 6, 2026, was published with the word "update" added to its headline and with one technical detail changed. The earlier version said Quantum Shroud protects data in motion in six independent layers, while the later version drops that count and describes the protection in general terms.

The partnership centers on two products. Greenlight is a passwordless, image-based sign-in tool that does not rely on passwords, one-time codes or push approvals, which the announcement says attackers can steal or replay. It completes authentication on the device, so users can log in even in denied, disconnected, intermittent or low-bandwidth environments, and it integrates with Microsoft Entra ID and CAC/PIV credentials. Quantum Shroud and Quantum Guard use NIST-standardized post-quantum cryptography, specifically FIPS 203 ML-KEM and FIPS 204 ML-DSA, to protect data in motion at enclave boundaries and data on devices, respectively. The release says these tools are meant to help agencies move toward Zero Trust and CNSA 2.0 timelines without modifying existing systems.

Scott Monfredo, Vice President of Government Programs at RJ Lee Group, said the partnership would put the company's security portfolio in front of agencies that need it, and he pointed to federal mandates, including the DoW Zero Trust Strategy and OMB memoranda M-22-09 and M-26-15, that require phishing-resistant authentication and post-quantum cryptography on tight schedules. Rob Pickle, Sales Director overseeing RJ Lee Group at Carahsoft, said the products complement Carahsoft's cybersecurity offerings and will be made more accessible to government agencies through reseller partners and contract vehicles. The release says RJ Lee Group is a small business with four decades of service to government and commercial clients, and that it maintains a NIST SP 800-171-aligned program with CMMC Level 2 posture. The announcement does not describe any further steps or timelines beyond availability through the listed contracts, SEWP V contracts NNG15SC03B and NNG15SC27B and E&I Contract #EI00063~2021MA.

stories.Headline: Incoming Democratic majorities put AI giants on notice
stories.Summary:
Incoming Democratic majorities said on November 4, 2026, that the era of Republican-led Washington taking a hands-off approach to artificial intelligence is ending. Voters in the 2026 midterm elections chose Democratic candidates who campaigned on legal guardrails for AI, and dozens of state and local ballot measures restricted new data center construction. According to SSRS exit polling, 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their votes for Congress. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the midterms, which shifted the balance of power in Washington. The ballot results were widely read as a mandate for change.

At a post-election press conference with House Democratic leaders, Representative Ted Lieu of California outlined what Democrats plan to do next term. He said they will hold public hearings on AI and pass reasonable guardrails for the technology. Lieu co-chairs a House Democratic commission on AI, which Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries formed last year. He said he and his colleagues will release a document laying out policy priorities for the new Congress.

Several Democratic senators-elect campaigned on specific AI ideas, including a two-year moratorium on data centers in South Carolina and requirements that data centers cover the full cost of their energy use in North Carolina. Texas Senator-elect James Talarico said he wants to prioritize youth safety. Lieu blamed the Trump administration and House Republicans for last year's decision to let the AI industry operate largely without limits, calling it a poor choice both politically and on policy. OpenAI responded less than 48 hours after Election Day by announcing new commitments for its data centers, including covering energy costs and investing in jobs.

The company said voluntary commitments were an important starting point but that clear rules from federal, state, and local policymakers were needed to build trust between communities, elected officials, and companies. Democrats are expected to push for rules that go well beyond such voluntary standards. Because their majorities are not large enough to override a veto, any new law would still face President Donald Trump, who has opposed AI regulation and supports data centers. The article suggests voters' rejection of Republican policies could push him toward compromise.

stories.Headline: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Boom Is Far From Over. Here Are 4 Potential Long-Term Winners
stories.Summary:
A Motley Fool analyst, Prosper Junior Bakiny, argued on November 7, 2026 that the boom in artificial intelligence still has years to run, pointing to recent earnings from major AI companies that show continued spending on AI infrastructure. He named four companies he sees as positioned to benefit over the long term: Nvidia, Microsoft, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom. The piece was published on Fool.com and was syndicated by The Globe and Mail the same day. The author's central claim is that corporations are backing their talk about AI spending with real money, which he takes as evidence the AI revolution is far from finished.

Nvidia, the author says, has built a lead in graphics processing units that is hard to overcome, helped by its CUDA software ecosystem, which makes it costly for customers to switch. He acknowledges that demand for GPUs may not grow as quickly as it has recently, but notes the company has moved into adjacent hardware and services that work with its chips for training and running AI models. Microsoft is described as having adapted after some investors worried that AI would make its software obsolete, with its cloud business booming partly because of its AI services and a rapidly growing cloud backlog. The article also credits Microsoft's steady revenue, strong cash position and innovation as reasons it could keep tapping the AI market.

Advanced Micro Devices, the author writes, has been a distant second to Nvidia in GPUs but is now seeing strong demand for central processing units, particularly in its data center business, and he suggests AI agents that run on CPUs could be a lasting tailwind. He notes the company has raised its 2030 total addressable opportunity guidance several times in the past year, and he cites its technological expertise, corporate relationships and switching costs as advantages. Broadcom is presented as a leader in custom AI chips, which some corporations are turning to as a cheaper and more power-efficient alternative to GPUs. The author says Broadcom counts major AI companies among its relationships, including Meta, Alphabet and Anthropic, and that its AI chip business carries lower margins than its software segment but should still support solid long-term growth.

The article is an opinion-based stock recommendation rather than a report on any single event, and it closes with a note that its figures reflect market data as of the publication date. The companies' share prices and market values shown on the page are presented alongside the text, though the article itself does not forecast specific returns. The Globe and Mail's version adds a disclaimer that it has not reviewed the syndicated content and includes promotional material from The Motley Fool. The author holds positions in Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia, and The Motley Fool holds positions in and recommends several of the companies discussed.

stories.Headline: Amazon’s AI Spending is Pressuring Free Cash Flow. Is the Stock Still a Buy?
stories.Summary:
In early November 2026, The Motley Fool published an analysis by Adria Cimino asking whether Amazon's stock remains a buy despite heavy spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure. The piece was carried on Yahoo Finance on November 7, 2026, and on Fool.com the same day. It notes that Amazon Web Services is the world's largest cloud provider and that the company's core retail business and its AI businesses are both pushing revenue to record levels. In the third quarter, AWS reached an annual revenue run rate of $184 billion, with quarterly revenue up 39% to $46 billion, the fastest growth in almost five years.

The article explains that Amazon must make large investments to meet current demand and prepare for future demand. The company forecasts $220 billion in capital spending for the full year, which has put pressure on free cash flow. In the third quarter, Amazon reported negative free cash flow of more than $42 billion over the trailing twelve months, driven by purchases of property and equipment. The company also lifted its capex forecast by $20 billion during the second quarter, while keeping the full-year forecast unchanged in the third quarter. Amazon's chief executive, Andy Jassy, said on the second-quarter earnings call that the free cash flow headwinds would continue until the new data centers are running, and that spending occurs about two years before monetization begins.

The author argues that the spending is necessary if Amazon wants to keep its lead in AI, and points to AWS growth as evidence the investment has paid off. stories.Headline: Opinion | US and China must join hands to measure rising AI tide
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is advancing so quickly that Washington and Beijing may not have a shared sense of how fast its capabilities are growing, according to an opinion piece by Marshall Li and Zhengfei Zhang published by the South China Morning Post on November 7, 2026. The authors argue that the next US-China talks on AI should start by asking whether both governments really understand this pace. They say the two sides need a common method for measuring progress before deciding how to respond. The piece notes that Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet in Shenzhen soon, with AI likely to stay high on their agenda.

The authors describe their ongoing exchanges on the technology as a positive sign, though they warn that governments may have less time to prepare for its consequences than they assume. They point to changes in creative and professional work, where AI is reshaping fields once thought hard to disrupt. In China, according to the article, more than 90 per cent of new microdramas released in the first eight months of the year were AI-generated, produced without cameras or live actors. A production that once needed as many as 100 people can now be finished in one week by a team of two to five. The authors add that AI has eliminated much of the well-paid work that actors once relied on.

The article frames the call for shared measurement as a responsibility of both governments rather than of any single party. It presents Li and Zhang as arguing that Beijing and Washington should work together to track how quickly the technology is progressing. The authors' central request is that the two governments first agree on a basis for judging AI's development and only then decide on policy. The piece does not describe any formal commitment or agreement reached by either government on this point. It instead positions the proposal as a step toward closing the gap between the speed of AI's advance and the speed of official responses.
