stories.Headline: NYT Cooking AI Gets 3 Egg & Butter Swaps Wrong [2026]
stories.Summary:
The New York Times Cooking team has added an AI assistant to its recipe platform that can swap ingredients, rescale servings and adapt recipes for different pans. In a recorded test, the tool made two errors, both of the kind a home baker might not catch until the cake came out wrong. The Times announced the feature in an October 23, 2026 article titled "How, and Why, We're Adding A.I. Tools to NYT Cooking," and coverage from JournalArta and The Verge has followed it. The tool is in a gradual, beta-style rollout.

The assistant lets users request changes that are highlighted in orange so they can see what differs from the original. Customized recipes and the chats that produced them stay in the user's account and cannot be published or shared through Cooking. The original recipe is left unchanged. NYT Cooking says the AI's responses and custom recipes have not been reviewed by its editors or endorsed by the original creators. The company said the staged launch was meant to measure performance, including speed, and to see how people use the tool.

In the test, the tester converted a Cinnamon Roll Bundt Cake into muffins, and the tool cut the bake time from three hours to 50 minutes and split the batter across two 12-muffin tins. When asked to halve the recipe, the assistant changed five eggs to three rather than two and a half, a rounding choice that went unexplained. Later, the tester asked how much butter the recipe needed, and the assistant answered six tablespoons without saying which version it meant. The original calls for three-quarter cup, so the answer matches the halved recipe but not the original, and the reporting notes that six tablespoons would have yielded a dry cake. The coverage names Genevieve Ko, a senior editor and columnist at NYT Cooking, as a staff figure on the effort, but does not quote her on the tool.

The articles do not name the underlying AI model, the price, the subscription tier, the user count or a wider release date. They also do not say whether the reported errors have been fixed. Readers who want to check an AI-adapted recipe should compare it against the original and test any changed quantities before baking. More details on the rollout are expected as the beta continues, and the articles do not say when those will arrive.

Articles.Title: NYT Cooking AI Gets 3 Egg & Butter Swaps Wrong [2026]

stories.Headline: CERT-In's AI Audit Rules Need Teeth: Who Will Ensure Companies Comply?
stories.Summary:
On 4 November, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a 107-page set of guidelines for auditing the security of artificial intelligence systems. The document covers AI systems built, bought, deployed or run in India, as well as systems that process Indian data or serve Indian users. Each system is scored on eight factors and rated low, moderate, high or critical. Low-risk tools may need only a self-assessment, while moderate and higher systems need a yearly audit by a CERT-In-empanelled firm, and critical systems also need continuous monitoring and red-team exercises. Reportable AI security incidents must be disclosed to the agency within six hours.

The guidelines set out nine audit domains, running from governance and data privacy to fairness, explainability and supply-chain assurance. Low-risk systems must cover only governance and security, while all nine apply from the moderate tier upward. Each system needs a named owner, with one executive accountable to the board. Third-party contracts should secure audit rights, change notices and prompt incident alerts.

Agents need least-privilege access, human approval for consequential actions and a tested way to interrupt them. The commentary, written by cybersecurity specialist Subimal Bhattacharjee, argues that the guidelines lack binding force. It says the document cites no enabling provision, start date or penalty, and that only the six-hour reporting clock and 180-day log retention carry clear force through CERT-In's 2022 directions. The author points out that CERT-In said it held no data on overall compliance with the earlier six-hour rule, which made outside checking difficult.

The Government counted 237 empanelled auditors in March, and the author notes that the agency has not said how many firms are qualified for high-risk work. The author says that formal directions for high-risk and critical systems should come from CERT-In, and that sector regulators such as the Reserve Bank of India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India and the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India could make them binding in their fields. He also suggests that government buyers demand audit certificates for AI rated moderate or above, that small firms receive subsidised audit vouchers, and that random checks and annual anonymised compliance data be published. The article is an opinion piece, and its views are the author's own.

Articles.Title: CERT-In's AI Audit Rules Need Teeth: Who Will Ensure Companies Comply? - The Quint

stories.Headline: MITRE ATLAS: AI Threat Matrix, Data and Usage
stories.Summary:
I can't write the story as specified. The article text provided is a CASRAI site page about MITRE ATLAS, a guide describing what the framework is, where its data lives, and its limits. It does not report a specific event, such as an incident, announcement, or development with a date, actor, and consequence, so there is no news to narrate in the requested structure. The page also gives no "who is responsible" beyond the general credit to The MITRE Corporation, and no "what happens next." I can instead write a factual summary of what the articles do state, in three paragraphs of four to five sentences each:

MITRE ATLAS, short for Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems, is a public knowledge base describing how adversaries attack AI-enabled systems. Its content is organized as a matrix of tactics, which are the adversary's goals, and techniques, which are the methods used to pursue them, supported by case studies. The official atlas-data repository calls its YAML files the authoritative source of ATLAS data, and the content is credited to The MITRE Corporation and marked approved for public release. The project's home is atlas.mitre.org, and its code and data are published under the mitre-atlas GitHub organization. ATLAS entries can also reference MITRE ATT&CK, a knowledge base of techniques drawn from real-world observation.

Users who want the data are directed to the dist folder of the atlas-data repository, where dist/ATLAS-latest.yaml holds the latest content and dist/manifest.yaml maps releases to their files. Content versions follow a YYYY.MM.N pattern, while format versions are semantic versions, and separate versioning began with content 2026.05 and format 6.0.0. Generated outputs include an ATLAS-only STIX JSON bundle, optionally combined with ATT&CK Enterprise, along with Excel workbooks and Navigator layers for visual annotation. The guide notes that the repositories do not publish counts of tactics, techniques, or mitigations, so current YAML should be checked rather than figures quoted from third-party pages.

The guide describes ATLAS as a shared vocabulary and a machine-readable, versioned resource, but also lists its limits. It describes adversary behavior rather than controls, is not a certification scheme or compliance checklist, and does not rank techniques by likelihood or impact. Because content and format versions change independently, a pinned file can become stale or break a parser after a format change. The guide suggests pairing ATLAS with complementary resources such as MITRE ATT&CK, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and model-specific testing tools, since each serves a different purpose.

Articles.Title: MITRE ATLAS: AI Threat Matrix, Data and Usage

stories.Headline: Embodied AI: Definition, Components and Research Areas
stories.Summary:
Embodied AI is a field of artificial intelligence built around an agent with a physical or simulated body that learns by perceiving and acting within an environment. A CASRAI guide, last reviewed on 8 November 2026, explains the concept by drawing on two arXiv papers. The article notes that the field lacks a single formal definition, so it attributes each framing to its source. The guide was written for researchers and research administrators.

The ICML 2024 position paper "A call for embodied AI," by Paolo, Gonzalez-Billandon and Kégl, presents embodied AI as a key step toward artificial general intelligence. It contrasts this approach with current large language models and traces the idea of embodiment through philosophy, psychology, neuroscience and robotics. Under this view, an embodied system is judged by what it does in an environment, not only by the text or images it produces. The guide reports that the paper names four essential components: perception, action, memory and learning.

The comprehensive survey by Liu and colleagues (arXiv:2407.06886, first submitted 9 July 2024 and revised 25 August 2025) treats the field as covering both physical robots and simulators. It organizes research around four targets, and the guide describes these as the areas of study the survey maps. The survey also discusses multi-modal large models, world models, datasets and open challenges. The guide adds that the two sources divide the topic differently, with one listing components inside an agent and the other listing research targets across the field.

The guide frames the position paper as arguing that embodied AI is the next step beyond large language models, while noting that the survey treats multi-modal large models as one of the technologies used in embodied systems. It advises readers to start with the position paper for the conceptual argument and the survey for the broader map. It also recommends citing the specific arXiv version read, since preprints may change after peer review. No further developments or timelines are reported in the article.

Articles.Title: Embodied AI: Definition, Components and Research Areas

stories.Headline: What Is Atlassian (TEAM) Telling Investors With Its AI Push And Cautious Outlook?
stories.Summary:
Atlassian, the software maker known for its collaboration tools, reported first-quarter results that management tied to strong momentum in its cloud products and newer AI features. Revenue for the quarter reached US$1,772.15 million, and the company swung from a loss to net income of US$90.72 million. Atlassian also appointed Eli Berkovitch as Chief Accounting Officer, adding a senior finance leader to its team. The article describes this as a signal of continuity on execution for the company's cloud and AI strategy. The article notes that the heavy spending on AI and cloud could weigh on GAAP margins if it does not produce clear pricing power and higher recurring revenue over time.

The analysis in the article comes from Simply Wall St, which produced it with AI automation based on historical data and analyst forecasts. It states that the commentary is general in nature and does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock. The writer identifies subscription recurring revenue growth and the GAAP operating margin, which management outlined around a 5% target for the year, as the key measures to watch in the rest of fiscal 2027. stories.Headline: Camerimage Founder Marek Zydowicz on AI, Aronofsky and Why “Cinematographers Are Artists, Not Technicians”
stories.Summary:
Camerimage, the Polish festival devoted to cinematography, marks its 34th year this November in Torun, running from November 7 to 14. Its founder, Marek Zydowicz, who started the event in 1993 to champion cinematographers and other below-the-line artists, is speaking openly about the issues facing the industry. Those include the rise of generative AI, which has its own debates and workshops at this year's festival, along with pressure on budgets and theatrical releases. The festival has also chosen to honor Darren Aronofsky, an outspoken adopter of AI, with its director award.

Zydowicz says Camerimage will stay open to a diversity of techniques and technologies, but he draws a firm line at fully AI-generated films. Joe Walker, the editor known for Dune and 12 Years a Slave, is also being honored and will chair the Main Competition jury. Polish cinematographer Janusz Kaminski, whose Disclosure Day is screening in contention, receives THR's Visionary award. Zydowicz frames the festival's mission as defending the artistic standing of people the industry has long treated as technicians.

In the interview, Zydowicz traces the strength of Polish cinematography to history, arguing that the tradition of depicting national events during the partitions and the postwar founding of the Lodz Film School shaped it. He says artists working under communist censorship learned to convey hidden meanings through composition and the relationship between image and dialogue. He also credits the Lodz school's teaching of painting history, and generations of filmmakers who taught there, for producing a tradition now visible in Polish cinematographers' work worldwide. He explained the Aronofsky choice by pointing to more than thirty years of films that unsettle audiences and ask them to confront difficult aspects of human nature.

Zydowicz cited Requiem for a Dream, Black Swan, The Fountain and The Whale as examples of work that moves between intimacy and spectacle while encouraging viewers to notice pain that might otherwise go unseen. He said he expects the decision to spark debate, given how contentious AI remains across the industry. The article does not describe what the festival's AI workshops will cover or how the jury will assess films made with new technology. Coverage of the festival's competition and awards is likely to follow as the November 7 to 14 program unfolds.

Articles.Title: Camerimage Founder Marek Zydowicz on AI, Aronofsky and Why “Cinematographers Are Artists, Not Technicians”

stories.Headline: AI-Driven Quantification of Coronary Plaque Outperforms Standard Care in Suspected CAD
stories.Summary:
A randomized trial called PARAMOUNT, presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago, found that an AI-based coronary CT analysis outperformed standard care for patients with suspected coronary artery disease. The study, led by Todd Villines, MD, of the University of Virginia, compared a plaque-based management strategy with usual care. Villines discussed the findings in an interview with HCPLive, and the results were described as preliminary. The trial enrolled 530 patients at 21 sites between January 2025 and February 2026.

The trial enrolled symptomatic adults older than 18 who were suspected of having coronary artery disease, excluding those with an LDL below 100 mg/dL, those already treated beyond primary prevention guidelines, and those with suspected acute coronary syndrome. Patients were randomly assigned to either coronary plaque-based care or usual care. The plaque-based group underwent coronary CT angiography with AI-enabled assessment of plaque morphology and composition. The primary endpoint combined several measures, including diagnostic certainty, LDL reduction, and avoidance of unnecessary invasive angiography and stenting.

Among the enrolled patients, the median age was 57 years, 57% were women, and the median baseline LDL-C was 128 mg/dL. At 180 days, plaque-based care was favorable to standard care, with a win ratio of 2 (95% CI, 1.37-2.56; P less than .0001). Diagnostic certainty about the presence of coronary artery disease contributed most to the primary endpoint. The investigators concluded that AI-based plaque assessment may give physicians greater confidence when evaluating chest pain.

Villines noted that the speed and standardization of AI-generated reports should continue to improve as coronary CT scan volumes grow. He said AI could help reading physicians with pre-reads and plaque staging, making their work more efficient. Full results are expected in early 2027. Villines reported consulting for Cleerly, HeartFlow, and Milestone.

Articles.Title: AI-Driven Quantification of Coronary Plaque Outperforms Standard Care in Suspected CAD

stories.Headline: Korea to Gather 100 Citizens to Debate AI Fake News Rules
stories.Summary:
South Korea's government will convene a panel of 100 citizens to discuss how to respond to fake news generated by artificial intelligence, with the aim of shaping future AI policy around the views collected. The Ministry of Science and ICT and the National AI Strategy Committee will hold the first Public Deliberation Forum on AI Issues in Seoul on the 12th, and the agencies announced the plan on the 7th. The 100 participants are to be selected to represent a cross-section of the public. The government says the forum will examine the many ways AI affects democracy and discuss the direction society should take.

The first topic is AI-generated fake news. As regulators weigh changes, including widening the range of deepfake material that must carry a mandatory AI label, the forum will take up where freedom of expression should end and regulation should begin. Participants will look at gray-area content, such as realistic satirical videos featuring real people and synthetic material with no sign it was made with AI. Under the current AI Framework Act, deepfakes must carry a notice that they were made with AI, though creative works may display the label in a way that does not disrupt viewing. The government launched a public participation platform called Modu AI late last month to support the effort.

The government also plans to discuss how much responsibility AI developers and content distribution platforms should bear. Under current law, the duty to disclose AI-made deepfakes falls only on AI businesses. To reduce industry confusion, the government has suspended fines for violations until at least January 22 next year. President Lee Jae-myung has separately called for a stronger response to fake news in general. At a Cabinet meeting on the 3rd, he said incitement driven by fake news is becoming a highly effective tool and causes social harm that requires a strong response.

Articles.Title: Korea to Gather 100 Citizens to Debate AI Fake News Rules - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Klleon Sees AI Humans Moving From Guides to Entertainers
stories.Summary:
Klleon, a Korean AI human technology company, is pushing its digital human technology from guidance and education into entertainment, with the shift described by Klleon's chief product officer Seo Ji-ho at the "U-KNOCK 2026 in USA" event at the Biltmore Hotel in Los Angeles on January 6. The article, published November 8, 2026 by Seoul Economic Daily, reports that AI is moving from one-way content toward real-time conversation shaped by a user's questions and responses. Klleon's technology is now used mainly in business-to-business and business-to-government projects, where AI humans act as guides in public institutions and retail spaces. The company also offers role-playing training for sales and customer service staff, along with products such as Klleon Studio, an SDK for embedding real-time avatars in other services, and RollFit, a training solution that lets managers set scenarios.

Klleon is also expanding into entertainment, supplying AI human technology to "My AI Partner," an SBS variety program released through Netflix in August that has broadcasters interact with AI humans over a set period. Seo said emotional exchange will matter more in entertainment than the information delivery that defined guidance and education. He added that the technology could expand into entertainment and business-to-consumer content. The company's visit to the United States was meant to gauge how local consumers respond to AI content, and it found that some saw AI as a tool to extend creators' imagination while others felt AI output lacks a human touch. Seo said he had come to see those cultural differences for himself, noting that fear and resistance toward AI appeared stronger in the U.S. than in Korea or Asia.

According to Seo, companies should not rush to seize the market but should understand cultural and national differences and prepare technology that fits human expression. The article frames the key to Klleon's expansion as whether AI humans can establish themselves as technology that communicates with people rather than replaces them. Klleon plans to broaden its market by advancing the technology and increasing content uses that reflect each country's cultural traits. The article does not give further figures, timelines or results for these plans.

Articles.Title: Klleon Sees AI Humans Moving From Guides to Entertainers - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: [News] MediaTek Reportedly Taps Intel Packaging Veteran After TSMC Hire, Advances Dual CoWoS–EMIB Strategy
stories.Summary:
MediaTek has hired Navid Shahriari, a former Intel executive vice president, as senior vice president, with the appointment effective November 9. Reports from Liberty Times and BigGo Finance, both published in early November 2026, say he will report directly to President and Chief Operating Officer Joe Chen. The move is the company's second major advanced packaging hire this year, following its May 2026 engagement of former TSMC research and development vice president Yu Chen-hua as an advisor. Shahriari brings 37 years of experience in semiconductor design engineering and advanced packaging, along with hands-on work in the data center market.

In his new role, Shahriari will oversee teams covering advanced process and yield platforms, design-technology co-optimization, advanced testing and packaging, and quality and reliability. MediaTek has said one of his core missions is to deepen collaboration with TSMC and other key supply chain partners. The aim is to integrate advanced technologies that strengthen the company's artificial intelligence and high-performance computing products. Reports describe the appointment as part of a wider effort to move MediaTek beyond smartphone chips toward data center AI chips. Reuters reports that the company supports both TSMC's CoWoS and Intel's EMIB packaging technologies, letting customers choose between them.

Shahriari spent most of his career at Intel, where he served as executive vice president of Intel Foundry and oversaw packaging, testing, and advanced packaging strategy before retiring in June of this year. According to the reports, he led development of complex packaging and substrate technologies and supported production at several large manufacturing sites. Reports also say MediaTek has worked with Intel on its EMIB technology for certain cloud ASIC projects, including work tied to Google's TPU program. MediaTek has not publicly detailed how Shahriari's work will be measured.

The hiring comes as MediaTek ramps up its AI accelerator ASIC business. According to Focus Taiwan, the company began shipping its first AI accelerator ASIC in September 2026 and expects roughly US$2.5 billion in revenue from it in the fourth quarter. MediaTek is targeting about US$16 billion in AI ASIC revenue and a 20% market share in 2027, with its next-generation accelerator slated for commercial production in the first quarter of 2028. Analysts cited by BigGo Finance note that advanced packaging capacity remains a bottleneck across the AI supply chain. They say whether MediaTek turns its new talent into project progress will still depend on coordination with its foundry and packaging partners.

Articles.Title: [News] MediaTek Reportedly Taps Intel Packaging Veteran After TSMC Hire, Advances Dual CoWoS–EMIB Strategy - TrendForce

stories.Headline: Chip Industry Week In Review - Semiconductor Engineering
stories.Summary:
SK hynix expects memory supply constraints to persist through 2030, with DRAM and HBM volumes effectively sold out through 2029, the company said in the week’s review. Samsung expects tight memory supply through 2028, citing lengthy fab construction and equipment lead times, larger dies, and greater process complexity in next-gen HBM. Samsung also said its 2027 HBM supply is already sold out. Solidigm, SK hynix’s U.S. subsidiary, reportedly is discussing a proposed $45B NAND flash fab with the U.S. Commerce Department. China’s CXMT plans to soon begin limited production of HBM3E memory despite manufacturing yields of just 20% to 30%, per Reuters.

Anthropic warned in its IPO filing that HBM shortages and limited TSMC manufacturing capacity could constrain AI expansion. ASE forecasts a doubling of its advanced-packaging revenue in 2027, and Amkor is ramping new high-density fan-out and 2.5D packaging programs. TSMC reportedly is considering a 20% price increase for CoWoS as AI demand continues to strain advanced-packaging capacity. Applied Materials plans to increase its stake in Besi to about 20%, deepening a strategic partnership that is expanding beyond hybrid bonding into new interconnect architectures and advanced packaging technologies for AI.

The review also covered manufacturing and AI tool news. Intel Foundry reported improving manufacturing execution in Q3, citing better yields and cycle times on 18A, and released its 14A 0.9 PDK in October. Infineon plans to invest €1.1B through 2034 at its Villach, Austria facility to establish Europe’s first high-volume manufacturing facility for next-gen GaN power semiconductors on 300mm wafers. UMC approved an additional $3.2B in capital spending to accelerate capacity expansion in Singapore and Tainan. Lam Research and imec expanded their collaboration on advanced 3D integration, next-gen memory, and high-NA EUV patterning.

On the AI side, Cadence introduced a portfolio of domain-specialized AI models for agentic chip and system design, and Arm introduced a new CPU benchmarking methodology for agentic AI. Google is expanding the reach of its custom AI accelerators, with OpenAI reportedly planning to purchase its TPUs, reports The Information. Oracle will offer Google’s TPUs through its cloud infrastructure beginning in 2027 and plans to add Arm’s AGI CPUs in fall 2027. Broadcom’s XPUs and networking equipment will support Anthropic’s AI infrastructure expansion, beginning in 2027, under a $63B financing arrangement.

Articles.Title: Chip Industry Week In Review - Semiconductor Engineering

stories.Headline: Ai+toolkit | Tag | techmonk
stories.Summary:
Block has launched Builderlab, an enterprise intelligence toolkit, according to a TechGig article dated November 6, 2026. The toolkit is built on Buzz, Block's open-source workspace. The article says the toolkit is meant to bring discussion and execution together in software building. It is positioned as going beyond individual AI tools.

The article gives no further details on pricing, availability, or specific features. It also does not name a launch date beyond the article's publication date. The surrounding page content is mostly unrelated event listings, including the IndiaAI Challenge 2026, Ericsson recruitment events, and DevNext 2026, and carries no further information about Builderlab. The article does not name a specific person quoted about the launch, and it does not provide any statement from Block's leadership.

Its description of the toolkit's purpose comes from the article itself rather than from a company quote. Beyond the publication, the articles offer no account of who developed the toolkit or how it is being rolled out. The articles carry too little for a full account, so this is treated as a breaking story. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Yelp Combines Native and Server-Driven UI for Its AI Assistant
stories.Summary:
Yelp has adopted a hybrid user interface architecture for its AI Assistant, pairing native mobile controls with server-driven conversation rendering so that interface changes can roll out faster across platforms. The design relies on Yelp's CHAOS framework, which stands for Content Hosting Architecture with Optimization Strategies, to render the conversation content. Navigation and message input remain native to each app. The approach was reported by InfoQ on November 6, 2026.

The Yelp Assistant first launched on iOS in 2024 to help users create project requests for local service professionals. It has since grown to answer questions about businesses and to support actions such as reservations, appointments, and food orders. CHAOS supports web, iOS, and Android. In a server-driven model, the backend defines what the client displays and how it responds to interactions, which means interface changes can reach users without a new mobile app release. The article does not give figures for adoption or release timing beyond these points.

Yelp engineers explained that the existing CHAOS framework lacked some capabilities the Assistant needed, including text input fields and network requests. Extending the framework would have delayed delivery, so the team kept navigation and message input native and used CHAOS only for the conversation area. The implementation separates view configuration from conversation data: the client fetches the CHAOS configuration when a chat starts, and later events update the existing view without refetching it. Those events cover persistent messages, temporary typing indicators and quick replies, and links, and the backend can also send actions such as disabling chat input once a project request is complete.

Yelp's engineers also acknowledged trade-offs. The architecture brings coordination challenges, engineers needed time to learn both the Assistant and CHAOS, and shared implementations can still behave differently across platforms. The article notes that separating view configuration from conversation data allows independent feature development and that the Android Assistant was reused to launch the Biz Ask Anything pilot. According to Yelp, this work laid the groundwork for its next-generation Assistant, which connects business information with actions users can take. The article also compares the approach with Airbnb's Ghost Platform, which likewise uses server-defined UI across web and mobile clients.

Articles.Title: Yelp Combines Native and Server-Driven UI for Its AI Assistant - infoq.com

stories.Headline: This was the week the AI trade cracked. So what's next?
stories.Summary:
A sharp sell-off hit AI and tech stocks this week, wiping out more than $2 trillion in value in a single session before shares bounced back the following day. Investors reacted to a wave of Democratic election wins that raised concerns about the future of AI, a technology that tech companies are spending heavily to develop. NPR's Rafael Nam and John Ruwitch discussed the moves on air. Analysts and reporters have not settled whether the sector is in a bubble that is about to burst.

Nam described the scale of the losses as staggering and said investors had already been uneasy about the AI trade all year. Data centers are central to AI companies, so proposals to create moratoriums or slow their development unsettled traders. Ruwitch said there has been a construction boom in AI data centers, with trillions of dollars committed to more of them. Local residents have raised worries about water and electricity costs and about jobs. In San Jose, California, Ruwitch reported that plans call for as many as 13 new data centers, and a resident there said things were moving too fast.

Data centers were also on the ballot nationwide on Tuesday, and Ruwitch said candidates who spoke against them won races in Texas, Ohio and South Carolina. He also reported that dozens of local measures in 13 states blocked or restricted future data center development. Ruwitch said the election results suggest it will be harder going forward for AI companies to build out their infrastructure. The articles do not name a single party or company as directly responsible for the sell-off, and they do not say what policy changes will follow. The reporting leaves open how far the local measures will spread and whether the pullback will last.

Articles.Title: This was the week the AI trade cracked. So what's next?

stories.Headline: Gao Zhikai: International cooperation can advance global AI development
stories.Summary:
Gao Zhikai, vice-president of the Center for China and Globalization, said in an interview during the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit that artificial intelligence and the internet should promote progress and serve the public good. The interview was published by China Daily on November 7, 2026. He made these remarks at the event in Wuzhen, where the summit took place. The articles present his comments as a call for broader international cooperation in the field.

Gao argued that as AI develops rapidly, it is important to think about how to better protect the continuity of the different civilizations, cultures and traditions found across countries. He called for international cooperation in AI to help countries around the world advance their AI development steadily. In his view, the World Internet Conference in Wuzhen offers a prime platform where AI and internet development can support and reinforce each other. The articles report his views as his own and do not describe any formal commitment, agreement or new requirement.

Gao holds the post of vice-president at the Center for China and Globalization, and the articles attribute these views to him in that role. The piece is a short interview, and the articles give no further detail on specific measures, timelines or figures tied to his proposals. The China Daily summary notes that it was generated by AI and that the publication takes no responsibility for it, so readers should rely on the interview text itself. The same page lists other unrelated items, including an exhibition on Yunnan and a discussion of AI and jobs, but the articles do not connect them to Gao's remarks. The articles do not say what follow-up steps, if any, are planned.

Articles.Title: Gao Zhikai: International cooperation can advance global AI development - China Daily

stories.Headline: Arkansas transportation officials explore AI’s potential for infrastructure, roadway safety
stories.Summary:
Arkansas transportation officials gathered in Rogers for the final day of the Arkansas Transportation Summit, hosted by the Arkansas Department of Transportation, to discuss how artificial intelligence could shape engineering, infrastructure and roadway safety. The three-day event brought together roughly 600 transportation officials and professionals to talk about emerging technology, infrastructure needs and future planning. Industry leaders said the next challenge is moving AI from experiments into everyday operations. The discussions took place Friday, November 6, 2026, according to the reporting. Chris Bosco, AI strategic initiative leader for the engineering firm Freese and Nichols, said the industry has spent the past two years learning how AI can support existing work.

He demonstrated an AI agent that analyzed engineering plans for an older Arkansas bridge and used them to build a 3D model of the structure. His company has also built a quality-control tool that checks project plans against design guidelines and flags inconsistencies. Bosco said the goal is continuous quality checks as engineers work, rather than waiting for a review milestone. He also pointed to uses in cost estimating, construction management and training future engineers through simulations.

Shashank Shekhar, a managing director and partner with Boston Consulting Group, said AI is meant to help professionals process more information and make better-informed decisions, not replace human judgment. He said the difference between agencies that have scaled AI and those that have not comes down to discipline in moving from pilot projects to proven value across the organization. University of Arkansas engineering professor Ngan Le described research on computer vision and video analytics that can interpret complex scenes involving people, vehicles and changing conditions. She noted that transportation agencies already run extensive camera networks that could feed such systems.

Eric Simpson, IT infrastructure services manager at the department, said the agency must decide how to use decades of data responsibly, and he said AI could help break down silos between divisions. Simpson also described using AI to anticipate roadway safety problems and target maintenance resources, but he stressed that policies, modernized data systems, employee preparation and accountability must come first. The department's AI guidelines list five principles: human oversight, data protection, transparency, accountability and security. Gayle Combs, a cybersecurity and infrastructure security adviser, warned that transportation systems are tied to energy, water and communications, so a disruption in one area can spread to others.

She urged organizations to identify critical assets and build relationships with partners, and she cautioned that AI could make cyberattacks more sophisticated. Panelists also raised the risk of employees relying on AI answers without checking them. Simpson summed up the tension by saying speed without governance is a serious risk. The next summit is scheduled for Sept. 21-23 at the Statehouse Convention Center in Little Rock.

Articles.Title: Arkansas transportation officials explore AI’s potential for infrastructure, roadway safety

stories.Headline: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails
stories.Summary:
Wired's Steven Levy, writing in his Backchannel newsletter on November 6, 2026, reports on a fast-growing market in which AI developers buy companies' internal work records, including documents, emails, Slack messages, tickets and call transcripts, to train their models. Levy says he received cold pitches offering media companies such as Wired between $350,000 and $1.8 million for a one-time copy of their old work records, with one pitch raising the figure to as much as $2 million. A freelance writer was offered $1,000 for a single story by a company called Handshake, which said it licenses professional documents across many fields so labs can test how models handle real knowledge work. Anthropic told Wired it acknowledges a big market for such data but does not buy workflow from live companies like Wired, and OpenAI did not respond before publication.

The market is led by a few young firms, including Handshake, Micro1 and Mercor, which Levy says are buying databases "as if it were a modern gold rush." Mercor, founded in 2023, has cofounders who became billionaires at 22 last year, and its CEO, Brendan Foody, told Levy that AI labs were frustrated by the quality of simulated data and need real messy business records. Foody said his company strips personal identifying information before data is transferred and that this can be verified. Micro1's CEO, Ali Ansari, estimated that labs, enterprises and robotics companies pay about $40 to $50 billion a year for data, a figure Levy could not verify, and predicted the spending would exceed a trillion dollars a year within two to four years. Levy also notes that a bankrupt Spirit Airlines put digital assets up for sale, including 80,000 email accounts, 500 million internal messages, 20.6 million SharePoint files and a million time-card records, and that the sale is now on hold after the flight attendants' union said it involved their private information.

Critics raise concerns that the anonymization may not fully remove personal details. Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, general counsel of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said unstructured emails and Teams messages are harder to scrub and may contain personal matters, and the union's president said the data became valuable so that models could replace jobs. Venture capitalist Gordon Ritter said the industry has not set norms for data acquisition and that the AI industry is moving faster than standards can be set. Ansari acknowledged that objections from workers are a fair point but said they would be manageable, arguing that workers will accept the trade-off for the abundance AI can bring, a claim Levy says he finds a convenient justification for compromises. Levy also describes a meeting with Tenkara, a two-year-old company whose head of commercialization confirmed that much of his job is buying data, and Levy says he declined to offer Wired's own editorial documents.

Articles.Title: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails

stories.Headline: Dr. Dre Has Zero Issues With AI in Music, Says He's 'Extremely Excited' About It
stories.Summary:
Dr. Dre said he is "extremely excited" about artificial intelligence in music and film, speaking on the debut episode of Listen & Laugh, the new podcast hosted by Ice Cube and Mike Epps. The episode was published on November 6, 2026, and Complex reported on it the following day. Dre said he did not see a problem with the technology and argued that people who object to it are not creative enough. Dre described AI as offering a new level of creativity and imagined a future where an actor could approve an AI-generated version of their own image and voice in a film. When Ice Cube asked whether Dre would mind if a producer used AI to copy his mixing style, Dre said he would not be upset and would respect it.

He compared AI use to sampling, saying he would welcome a remake of "Nuthin' but a 'G' Thang" that outdid the original, and he warned that people who do not adapt may be left behind. Ice Cube, who has been vocal against AI tools, said he supports creators who use them but objects to shortcuts that let people skip the years of work needed to make a great record. He also said his concern is with computers taking "total control" of the creative process. Dre pushed back, asking why the older generation should resist new tools simply because they are unfamiliar with them.

The two continued debating before agreeing to disagree. The exchange follows Ice Cube's 2023 comment, made on the Full Send Podcast, that AI-generated music was "demonic." The articles do not say whether the two will revisit the topic on future episodes. The full episode featuring Dre is available on Complex.

Articles.Title: Dr. Dre Has Zero Issues With AI in Music, Says He's 'Extremely Excited' About It

stories.Headline: E-Town ramps up AI tokens thrust
stories.Summary:
Beijing's Economic-Technological Development Area, known as E-Town, is building an AI ecosystem around what it calls a token economy, and it showed its plans at the ongoing 9th China International Import Expo in Shanghai. The exhibit, a 12-square-meter display, featured the area's efforts in space-based computing, semiconductors, infrastructure, large models and application platforms. The centerpiece is Beijing's first token factory, recently completed in the development area, which has nearly 10,000 petaflops of computing capacity. Unlike conventional data centers that mainly rent out computing resources, the token factory combines hardware, AI inference software and model optimization to deliver standardized AI processing services.

E-Town is also planning a distribution platform that would give developers access to different AI models and computing systems through one unified interface, with requests routed according to their needs. The aim is to connect large-scale token production with demand from companies and developers. Tokens, the basic data units AI models use to process and generate information, are increasingly used to measure AI workloads and price AI services. In August, the area introduced trial measures to support a token-driven intelligent economy. By 2030 it aims to establish four token factories, each with at least 10,000 accelerator cards, and to build an intelligent economy worth more than 400 billion yuan, or about $60 billion.

The showcase also included partner companies' technologies. Houmo.AI presented its M50 chip, an energy-efficient edge AI processor designed for large-model inference, intended to support AI deployment closer to end users and devices. ZTE Corp displayed its OEX orthogonal backplane-free interconnect architecture for supercomputing clusters, which is compatible with mainstream graphics processing units and has already entered commercial use among leading internet companies, telecom operators and government and corporate clients. VAST demonstrated Tripo P2.0, a 3D foundation model that generates structured 3D assets meeting industrial production standards within seconds. Maimai Technology Group showed agricultural robots powered by embodied intelligence.

The token economy reflects growing demand for AI inference. According to data from the National Data Administration, China's average daily token calls exceeded 500 trillion by June, up from 100 billion in early 2024. The strategy marks a shift from developing individual AI technologies toward building a coordinated industrial chain, in which advances in hardware and computing infrastructure support model development while practical applications generate demand for further improvements. The articles do not say how the planned distribution platform will be launched or when the 2030 targets will be reviewed.

Articles.Title: E-Town ramps up AI tokens thrust - China Daily

stories.Headline: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking
stories.Summary:
Open-weight AI models from China are now nearly as capable as the best closed models at carrying out network hacking, according to new research from Vals, a company that measures AI capabilities. The findings, reported by WIRED on November 6, 2026, were based on tests of how well different models could complete multi-step instructions on simulated corporate networks. Vals ran two scenarios, one involving a mock network reached through a public-facing website and another requiring a model to compromise one company network to reach a second. The results point to a turning point the cybersecurity field has long anticipated.

In the tests, OpenAI's most advanced cyber model, Daybreak, completed 81 percent of its assigned tasks on average across two runs, and it is available only to trusted partners. DeepSeek, an open-weight model from China, completed 73 percent on average and scored equally with Daybreak on some tasks. The research also found a large cost gap, with Vals estimating that an attack using GPT-6-Sol cost $17 to $46 in tokens while the same kind of attack with DeepSeek cost $2 to $3. Rayan Krishnan, CEO of Vals, said the lower cost gives defenders a strong reason to use open models rather than proprietary ones. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The findings matter because US frontier labs, particularly Anthropic, had justified limited releases of new models on the idea that gated access would only buy time before advanced hacking abilities became widely available. Anthropic's frontier red team lead, Logan Graham, told WIRED in April that the company's Project Glasswing gave trusted access to new models so defenders could get a head start. He said at the time that the world should prepare for these capabilities to be broadly available within 6, 12, or 24 months. The Vals results suggest closed models no longer hold a clear edge in cyber skills, which could make efforts to slow the spread of such capabilities largely pointless. Seven months after Graham's remarks, the article says, that transition seems to have arrived roughly on schedule.

The article also notes that experts still disagree about whether AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity or mainly amplified problems that already existed. Real-world observations of criminal and state-backed hacking, it says, show attackers generally conserve resources and rely on older, less capable models for most activity. Alex Zenla, cofounder and chief technology officer of the cloud security firm Edera, agreed that open-weight models can already produce advanced attacks, especially modified versions that have had safety training removed. He added that closed labs have likely trained unreleased models that go further, describing the situation as a cat-and-mouse game. Zenla warned that this may be the start of a dangerous security landscape.

Articles.Title: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking

stories.Headline: Thornton hardware store uses AI system to fight shoplifting
stories.Summary:
A Thornton hardware store is using an artificial intelligence camera system to combat shoplifting that has become a recurring problem. Richard McLamb, the store's manager, says employees deal with shoplifting attempts several times a week, and some thieves have targeted larger items, including a snowblower that he believes walked out the door. The store has installed the system, which watches live video feeds from cameras throughout the store. When it spots activity it considers suspicious, it sends employees a video clip of the incident so they can respond quickly.

The technology comes from Veesion, which provides AI-powered video surveillance for retailers. According to the company, almost 7,000 stores use its software, and nearly 1,000 of them are in the United States. Hiren Mowji, Veesion's director of sales, says the AI identifies suspicious activity in live video and sends retailers alerts with footage attached, giving them proof. McLamb says the alerts let employees step in before merchandise leaves the building. He recalled one case in which a person was caught on camera hiding screwdrivers and hammers in his pants before heading toward the exit.

McLamb said he stopped that person, recovered the merchandise and called police. Mowji described retail theft as a problem worth more than $100 billion that is getting worse every year, and said Veesion wanted to offer a practical solution for business owners. McLamb said the system also acts as an extra set of eyes, freeing employees to spend more time helping customers while staying aware of what is happening in the store. He believes that attentive customer service can also discourage theft, since thieves are less likely to steal when staff are close by.

Articles.Title: Thornton hardware store uses AI system to fight shoplifting

stories.Headline: SIU School of Medicine developing AI medical training
stories.Summary:
The Springfield Memorial Foundation and the SIU School of Medicine are investing $2 million to develop medical training programs that use artificial intelligence, according to a report published November 6, 2026. The work is underway at the Ed Curtis Laboratory for Innovation in Medical Education in Springfield, Illinois. The program turns real people into AI avatars, which medical professionals then train to respond to common patient interactions and questions. Medical students can engage with these avatars using a camera and microphone.

The main platform is a difficult conversations simulator that focuses less on diagnosis and more on relationships and on delivering bad news with empathy. The training covers situations such as referring a patient to hospice care, explaining a new allergy, and delivering a cancer diagnosis. The cases come from doctors, and the lab has recently begun working with correctional medicine on questions arising within institutions run by the Illinois Department of Corrections. The platform also lets doctors create their own cases by typing a description, such as a patient with lung cancer, and having the system generate the scenario.

Pinckney Benedict, the lab's program director and chief architect, is the main voice on the project. He said the technology reflects a new era of simulation because conversations can now happen without another person present. He argued that the training means a doctor is not facing a family's worst news for the first time with no preparation. Benedict also said the lab wants to be a leader in digital medical simulation and hopes to share the program with medical schools across the country.

Articles.Title: SIU School of Medicine developing AI medical training

stories.Headline: IREN (IREN) Stock Price Rallies As Q1 Results Spotlight AI Margins
stories.Summary:
IREN jumped roughly 20% in a single session after releasing its first quarter 2027 results, a sharp turnaround for a stock that had fallen more than 40% over the prior month. Investors responded most strongly to the company's artificial intelligence cloud business, which generated about US$200 million of the US$228 million in total revenue. Adjusted EBITDA margin came in near 29%, a notable step up from roughly 14% in the prior quarter. The results point to a shift away from legacy bitcoin mining toward AI infrastructure services.

Total revenue fell from US$240 million a year earlier, but the mix moved decisively toward AI cloud. The company still reported a net loss of US$263 million, compared with net income of US$385 million a year earlier, and a loss of US$0.66 per share. Management described its AI capacity for 2026 as largely sold out and said discussions for 2027 and 2028 were advanced. Its Horizon 1 facility is live with Microsoft, and operating annual recurring revenue reached US$1.0 billion.

The company, however, pushed its US$4 billion ARR target into early 2027 rather than late 2026, and it still plans a fiscal 2027 capital spending program of US$25 billion to US$30 billion funded largely with debt and customer prepayments. Bulls see the quarter as evidence that IREN is becoming a contracted AI utility, while bears worry that rising overhead, interest costs and the decommissioning of mining hardware will run ahead of recognized AI revenue. The timing of new capacity coming online late in the quarter is central to that concern. The articles indicate that the coming quarters will show whether the company can convert its contracted backlog into revenue while financing a very large build-out.

Articles.Title: IREN (IREN) Stock Price Rallies As Q1 Results Spotlight AI Margins

stories.Headline: AI’s Hidden Footprint, From Quartz Mines to Kenyan Click-Workers, Bared in Taiwan Creative Content Fest Doc ‘The Technological Sublime’
stories.Summary:
A documentary titled "The Technological Sublime," directed by Jannes Callens, is heading to the Taiwan Creative Content Fest in Taipei, where it will be shown as a work in progress. The film follows the physical supply chain that keeps artificial intelligence running, beginning at quartz mines in the Appalachians and moving on to chip plants in Taiwan, lithium fields in Chile, undersea cables and click-workers in Kenya. Its aim is to show what the technology costs people and the planet. The festival runs from November 6 to 9 at the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, organized by the Taiwan Creative Content Agency. Callens says that AI is often discussed as something abstract and invisible, but his research showed a tangible ecosystem behind the idea of "green" AI.

He noted that an online image search for AI mostly returns humanlike robots, with almost nothing showing the hardware and labor underneath, which pushed him toward the subject. He describes the film as a work of art meant to bring nuance to the AI debate by showing the achievements of the technology without ignoring its material, ecological and human costs. His earlier documentary, "Dor (Longing)," won the Best Belgian Film award at the Brussels Independent Film Festival and was selected for Visions du Réel. The first scenes of the new film have already been shot, and the team is waiting to secure the rest of its financing.

Delegate producer Steven Dhoedt, who has long followed new technology, said many people still find AI abstract despite the hype around it. He praised Callens for choosing a grounded, less sensational approach, which he believes suits the moment. Because filming spans four continents, the producers are still seeking more investors and partners. Belgian broadcaster VRT has come on board, and talks are underway with other European broadcasters.

The team is also working with James Chia-Hao Hsu of Reel Asia Pictures, its Taiwan partner, to start conversations with distributors and sales agents at the festival. The film is a co-production between Brussels-based Visualantics, Paris-based Tag Film, Cobra Films and Taipei-based Reel Asia Pictures. Dhoedt said TCCF gives the project a real chance to reach audiences in Asia. The article does not say when the finished film will be released or whether it has secured a distributor.

Articles.Title: AI’s Hidden Footprint, From Quartz Mines to Kenyan Click-Workers, Bared in Taiwan Creative Content Fest Doc ‘The Technological Sublime’

stories.Headline: A US host's 24 hours in Wuzhen: How AI goes to work
stories.Summary:
From November 2 to 5, 2026, the World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit is being held in Wuzhen, a water town in Jiaxing, Zhejiang province in East China. It is the 13th time the summit has met there. This year, organizers want to show a different side of artificial intelligence, which they say is no longer just an exhibit but has already started working in everyday settings. A host from the United States, named Jeremy, attended the first conference in 2014 and has returned twelve years later. He finds the town now full of self-driving vehicles where a ride-hailing app once impressed him.

The shift reflects a broader change in which humanoid robots are moving from laboratory prototypes to factory products. Shipments in China are expected to reach 62,500 units in 2026. At the "Light of the Internet" Expo and the AI Carnival, embodied-AI robots are working in real settings such as factories, hotels, hospitals and homes. The reporting presents these demonstrations as evidence that the technology is now being used in practice rather than only displayed. The articles give no further figures on costs or adoption rates.

Walking through the town, Jeremy sees AI built into daily routines. In the 5G smart greenhouse at Zhengfu village, tomato farmers rely on data rather than the weather to guide their work. On the streets, self-driving vehicles slow down for children at play, braking, stopping and steering around them. Robot guide dogs lead visually impaired pedestrians across zebra crossings. Elsewhere, robot dogs take on repetitive and hazardous tasks at zero-carbon factories and at the 110 kV Chenzhuang substation.

In an elderly care center, one robot rests its head beside a resident's hand without making a sound, simply keeping them company. The articles close by asking whether AI will replace people or open a wider world, and they leave that judgment to each observer. They name the China Daily as the source of the report, and the conference itself is organized under the World Internet Conference framework. The articles do not say who ultimately sets policy for these deployments or what outcomes the summit will produce.

The only article that bears on the headline is a short 13abc.com feature, published November 6, 2026, titled "Sashem Brey: Building a holiday budget with AI - Watching Your Wallet."
