stories.Headline: SK Hynix (KOSE:A000660) Unveils Cooler AI Memory As Data Center Scrutiny Grows
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, listed in Seoul as KOSE:A000660, introduced an iHBM low-heat memory design that it says is meant to reduce cooling demands in AI data centers. The company presented the new iHBM architecture as offering lower power use and less heat output than conventional high bandwidth memory used in AI servers. The announcement was reported on November 6, 2026, with the article published that day. Management framed the product as a response to growing scrutiny of the water and electricity consumed by data centers running AI workloads.

According to the report, the launch is also part of a broader effort to attract and retain chip engineers as Chinese competitors expand their hiring. The article describes SK hynix as a global memory and semiconductor supplier that makes chips for data centers, consumer devices and enterprise hardware. Any shift in its product mix toward lower power iHBM would therefore affect how AI infrastructure is built and cooled. The report does not give pricing, shipment dates or specific figures on power or heat savings.

The article is an AI-assisted analysis produced by Simply Wall St. and carried by Yahoo Finance, and it does not name a company official as a direct speaker. It states that management positioned iHBM as a response to scrutiny of data center water and electricity use, and that SK hynix highlighted the launch in connection with talent retention. The piece also says the company's long-term success depends on continued heavy capacity expansion, including new fabs and advanced packaging, while keeping its balance sheet disciplined. It stresses that it is general commentary and not investment advice.

The article presents the iHBM launch as a test of the bull case for SK hynix's heavy AI memory investment, since it targets power and cooling pressures in AI servers. It also notes the bear case that a custom low-heat design adds technical complexity and capital needs at a time when Chinese DRAM rivals are raising pay to recruit engineers. The report says nothing firm about what happens next beyond these competing considerations. It is also unclear from the article whether the iHBM design has begun commercial shipments.

Articles.Title: SK Hynix (KOSE:A000660) Unveils Cooler AI Memory As Data Center Scrutiny Grows

stories.Headline: Recently, the Ministry of Science and ICT launched the National AI Service Innovation Promotion Team..
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of Science and ICT has recently launched the National AI Service Innovation Promotion Team, a move that the article presents as a sign that all citizens will soon have access to artificial intelligence services. The writer, Professor Kim Eui-seok of the KAIST Graduate School of Technology Management, argues that skillful AI use is currently a rare advantage that will soon be widely shared. He compares this moment to the early spread of personal computers, when knowing Word and Excel set people apart until computers became standard on every desk. The article does not give dates, budgets, or staffing figures for the new team.

The writer's central claim is that once AI becomes a general-purpose infrastructure, like electricity or tap water, the ability to use it will no longer distinguish anyone for long. He draws on the former Harvard Business Review editor Nicholas Carr, who argued that what people create with technology matters more than the technology itself. In his view, lasting competitiveness will come from complementary assets such as human-centered judgment, unique experience, and trust. He points to two shifts: proof of processes replacing proof of results, with oral examinations and real-time demonstrations of reasoning becoming more valued, and a growing reliance on reputation and trust-based networks that AI cannot easily imitate. The writer makes these points as his own analysis rather than as reported government positions.

The article offers two practical habits for building these abilities. The first is to spend about 15 minutes on paper defining and structuring a problem before opening an AI tool, so that one's own thinking comes first. The second is to increase in-person meetings that build trust and teach people to handle conflict and coordination beyond algorithm-driven digital contact. The writer presents these as personal practices and does not describe any policy follow-up from the ministry.

Articles.Title: Recently, the Ministry of Science and ICT launched the National AI Service Innovation Promotion Team.. - 매일경제

stories.Headline: McDonald's will expand AI ordering to save 50 hours of labor weekly. Franchisees question the costs
stories.Summary:
McDonald's plans to expand its AI ordering system, Archy, to additional drive-thrus in the United States and Australia, according to Restaurant Dive. The company hopes the technology will save about 50 labor hours a week at its restaurants. CEO Chris Kempczinski announced the expansion during an earnings call, where he also said more overseas trials are scheduled for 2027. Most U.S. McDonald's restaurants are expected to receive the system, which takes voice orders in both Spanish and English.

The labor savings form part of a wider technology initiative that the company says is meant to raise restaurant margins by 2.5 percentage points. Archy sits alongside automated inventory tracking and connected equipment within the ArchIQ AI platform, which the chain announced in September as part of its Next initiative. During that September investor day, McDonald's reported that Archy's accuracy exceeded 90 percent and that customer satisfaction was high in early tests. Kempczinski said the technology would let staff focus on customer service and food quality, and he promised updates on Next throughout 2027.

Franchisees have raised doubts about whether the benefits will outweigh the costs. According to Peter Saleh, an analyst who covers restaurants and food distributors, operators said in October that the margin target seemed highly theoretical and that few details had been given about how productivity would improve. Saleh wrote that franchisees were most enthusiastic about the inventory management tools, which some believe could cut manager hours and food waste. Operators also questioned whether the consumer actually wants AI taking orders, and whether voice ordering fits with the company's renewed focus on service and hospitality.

The article places the expansion within a broader debate in the fast-food industry about automation and human service. Chick-fil-A has said its drive-thru orders will stay human-to-human even as rivals test AI, and McDonald's is retraining two million workers as chains reconsider kiosks and apps. The articles also note that AI systems depend on energy-hungry computing infrastructure that can strain resources and raise power bills. The articles do not say when the U.S. rollout will be complete, and they leave open how the costs will be split between the company and its franchisees.

Articles.Title: McDonald's will expand AI ordering to save 50 hours of labor weekly. Franchisees question the costs

stories.Headline: AI physics startup PSI says a system running a non-public Anthropic model proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a quantum computing question open since 2008 (PSI)
stories.Summary:
Physical Superintelligence (PSI), an AI physics startup, announced on November 6, 2026 that a research system developed in-house had proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a question in quantum computing open since 2008. The system ran on PSI's own infrastructure and used instances of a non-public Anthropic model. According to the company, the system produced a complete proof on the third day of the run, and the Lean proof assistant, which checks each step by computer, accepted it. The system then worked on related open problems and improved the result twice, with Lean accepting the final version.

The conjecture concerns whether quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones on random inputs, which lack the structure that powers speedups like Shor's algorithm from 1994. The articles describe the proof as showing that, if the conjecture holds, an ordinary computer can predict a quantum computer's answer to a yes-or-no question about a random string while reading far fewer bits than the quantum machine would need, so no exponential advantage exists unless the string has a rare pattern. The proof rests on a plan by Shachar Lovett and Jiapeng Zhang, in which one inequality had been left as a conjecture. The PSI team replaced that inequality with a new one proved in the manuscript, drawing on earlier work by David Reimer and several other researchers.

David Turturean, a Member of Technical Staff at PSI, led the work, developing the research system, scoping the problem and running it, and he is responsible for the correctness of the paper. Jim Halverson, an Advisor at PSI, audited the proof, and Phiala Shanahan, also an Advisor, commented on the Lean formalization. Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle and Li-Yang Tan of Stanford University had earlier, in August 2026, settled a special case of the conjecture, and they have since read the full proof, sent comments and are writing a shorter exposition for experts. They called the result a huge advance that resolves a decades-old conjecture. Earlier work had established weaker bounds or special cases only, and the articles say PSI's proof completes the full conjecture.

Articles.Title: AI physics startup PSI says a system running a non-public Anthropic model proved the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, a quantum computing question open since 2008 (PSI)

stories.Headline: 3 foreign nationals allegedly used AI to mimic CEOs in $129M scheme, DOJ says
stories.Summary:
Three foreign nationals have been charged in an alleged international fraud scheme that federal prosecutors say used AI to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys and steal more than $129 million. According to an indictment filed in the Southern District of New York, Jacob Soall was arrested in Spain in June, Sharon Hazan was arrested in Spain in August, and Guy Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. Prosecutors say the scheme ran from July 2024 to February 2026. The U.S. attorney's office says the group used the technology to copy the voices and images of company executives and attorneys at major law firms. The group allegedly targeted employees, typically in accounting departments, by telling them they were helping with a confidential financial transaction.

Using AI to mimic a chief executive's voice, the scheme then directed staff to contact supposed lawyers at large international law firms, who were in fact part of the operation. One participant would then instruct the employee to wire large sums to bank accounts set up around the world. The money was converted into cryptocurrency to hide its source and divided among the participants and their co-conspirators. Prosecutors allege the victims included an investment bank in New York, hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the U.K., a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida.

Prosecutors say Soall impersonated U.K. attorneys and used a script titled "Lawyer Call" to appear credible to victims. They also allege that Hazan handled laundering for the scheme and boasted that he had been doing so since 1994, claiming more than $400 million laundered in the past three years. Hazan was previously convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in the same district in 2008. Sheetrit is also accused of laundering funds.

All three face charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, two counts of aggravated identity theft, money laundering conspiracy and two counts of money laundering, and each charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in the release that the technology offers large potential but that some people seek to use it for crime. He urged individuals and businesses to consider how to protect themselves from what he called the emerging threat of AI-enabled crime, using the abbreviation SI, which he noted is the White House's preferred term for artificial intelligence. The articles do not say whether the defendants have entered pleas or obtained lawyers, or when they might be tried or extradited to the United States.

Articles.Title: 3 foreign nationals allegedly used AI to mimic CEOs in $129M scheme, DOJ says - NBC News

stories.Headline: AI Tool of the Week: this Gemini feature brings textbooks into AI learning
stories.Summary:
Google has added a feature to its Gemini Notebook, formerly known as NotebookLM, that lets students ask questions based on textbooks drawn from a built-in catalogue. The feature was described in a Mint article published on November 7, 2026, and Google's October 29 post says students can now access hundreds of textbooks from providers in the US and India. Answers come with inline citations and direct links to the original passages, so a student can check where the information comes from. The textbooks are free to use through the Add sources and Textbooks options within a notebook.

The feature addresses a problem the article describes: students who ask a general chatbot about a chapter may get confident answers that do not match the book their teacher follows, and they cannot easily verify them. Instead of downloading PDFs of the right edition, a student can select a book from the catalogue and ask questions grounded in it. Gemini Notebook can also turn a chapter into study guides, practice quizzes and flashcards. The article notes that the catalogue includes S Chand Publishing alongside OpenStax and the Open Textbook Library. It also says eligible ebooks bought on Google Play Books can already be added as sources.

The article was written by Jaspreet Bindra and Anuj Magazine, co-founders of AI&Beyond, as part of Mint's weekly "AI Tool of the Week" feature. It was excerpted from Leslie D'Monte's weekly TechTalk newsletter. The authors state that their tool recommendations are independent and based on their internal testing, and that the creators did not influence them. The article does not describe any response from Google beyond its October 29 post. It also does not say whether the catalogue will expand beyond the current set of providers or how schools and teachers are expected to adopt the tool.

Articles.Title: AI Tool of the Week: this Gemini feature brings textbooks into AI learning

stories.Headline: AI advising the White House? Why the task requires people—especially young folks
stories.Summary:
Jason Furman, a former chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under President Barack Obama and now a Harvard professor, recently said that if he were running the CEA today he would, somewhat regretfully, use current AI systems instead of hiring 20 human economists. He said the chair's job would be safe. After pushback, including from former staff, he softened his position and called for an AI-intensive CEA with only a skeleton staff. Under that version, he would still largely replace junior staff, recent college graduates and graduate students, with AI.

Furman based his argument on what AI can already do, pointing to a website he built called Econvitals that offers data dashboards, blog posts, memos, briefings and research papers. The author argues he is focusing on tasks rather than the organization's mission. The CEA, created in 1946, is meant to give the president objective economic advice on domestic and international policy. The author says its most important role is to stop bad ideas, and that AI models tend not to challenge them the way people do. Staff economists, many on leave from universities or detailed from the Federal Reserve or cabinet agencies, have less to lose by dissenting than political appointees.

The author, a Bloomberg Opinion columnist and former Federal Reserve economist, recalls working with junior staff who were often the first to notice when something did not add up. He describes a project his CEA year began with a magazine article about Americans unable to cover a $400 emergency expense, a finding that came from a Fed survey. Economists could not initially answer the president's question, and the work was creative rather than mechanical. The author says AI could speed data work and provide extra checks, and could help revisit researchers' views or tailor the Economic Report of the President to new audiences.

The author concludes that the CEA will change with AI, and that it should. He agrees with Furman that juniors spending their days overseeing bots would be a poor use of taxpayer money and talent, but argues that this reflects a choice about job design rather than a fact about AI. The same tools could free junior staff from monotonous data pulls and formatting so they can make quality improvements and pursue questions no one can yet answer. In the author's words, the president deserves a better CEA, not a smaller one.

Articles.Title: AI advising the White House? Why the task requires people—especially young folks

stories.Headline: Nvidia is driving the AI boom. Good
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, the American chipmaker whose graphics-processing units power artificial intelligence, has become the world's most valuable company, worth $5.4trn, according to an Economist analysis published by Mint on November 5, 2026. Its demand is described as insatiable, and the firm is projected to generate $370bn in net income next year and possibly reach $1trn in sales by 2029. The company's share price is said to be 14 times what it was when ChatGPT was released in late 2022. Nvidia alone accounts for 8% of the S&P 500, and the article notes that it has produced about 15 cents of every dollar the American stock market has returned since 2023.

The article describes a web of financing that has drawn comparisons to the dotcom era. Through $1trn-worth of deals, Nvidia provides cash or guarantees so that data-centre landlords and AI labs can buy its chips, and some critics call it the "bank of AI." Morgan Stanley estimates its overall credit exposure at $200bn by the start of 2029, which could later reach $300bn or more. The article also notes that Nvidia's share of research and development spending has fallen from over a fifth of sales to less than a tenth, while non-Nvidia AI chips now hold 38% of the market, up from 26% in 2023. Nvidia still keeps about $99bn in cash and expects to generate roughly $200bn this year.

The article's author argues that the worries are mostly unjustified and that the risks would fall largely on Nvidia's shareholders. It presents Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive, as a leader who believes the main obstacle to AI is insufficient infrastructure rather than weak demand, and who has concluded that the markets will not supply capital at the necessary scale. The article also reports that Goldman Sachs, BlackRock and Blackstone joined Nvidia last month in a $500bn data-centre initiative. It adds that AI revenue, from Anthropic and other firms and the hyperscalers, may now be around $150bn a year, far short of the $2.5trn needed for AI capital spending. The article concludes that if the bets fail, the costs will be borne mainly by investors, and if they succeed, the AI era may arrive sooner.

Articles.Title: Nvidia is driving the AI boom. Good

stories.Headline: AI-driven attacks put telecom security on govt radar
stories.Summary:
The Department of Telecommunications has stepped up efforts to protect India's telecom infrastructure from increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, including those powered by artificial intelligence. According to officials who spoke on condition of anonymity, the department has held several rounds of meetings with Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Reliance Jio and state-owned BSNL to strengthen network firewalls and other protective measures. The talks follow a series of advisories from the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warning about AI-enabled intrusions. The reporting, published on 6 November 2026, does not give a single date for the start of the meetings.

The department has mandated annual network security audits for telecom service providers, including vulnerability assessments and penetration testing. External network audits are required once every three years. DoT has also set up a telecom security operations centre to improve monitoring, situational awareness and coordination on cybersecurity. Separately, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India has proposed draft guidelines for the responsible use of AI in telecom networks, which call for risk-based classification of AI systems, human oversight, safety assessments and reporting of serious AI-related incidents to the regulator. Under the proposal, operators would remain accountable for AI systems they deploy, including those built or supplied by third parties.

A senior DoT official said the department is working with the operators and that the telcos are independently building security mechanisms, which the official described as robust. The official said the department has not seen any untoward incidents involving private operators or BSNL. The Cellular Operators Association of India had not responded to queries at the time of publication. CERT-In, in an advisory dated 15 October, flagged AI agents that gained unauthorised access to ICT assets of Indian organisations, and in a 4 November advisory it reported escalating AI-driven attacks on banking, financial services and insurance entities by a threat actor it calls Crafty Falcon.

The article places the Indian effort against wider global activity. It notes that Singapore disclosed in the previous year that all four of its major telecom operators had been targeted by a Chinese-linked group, and that Singapore announced further cybersecurity steps in March 2026. It also recalls the Salt Typhoon campaign that affected AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile in the United States, which came to light in 2024. The article does not say when the DoT's further talks with operators will conclude or when TRAI's draft framework will be finalised.

Articles.Title: AI-driven attacks put telecom security on govt radar

stories.Headline: Delhi HC orders takedown of AI-generated videos targeting CM Rekha Gupta
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 6, 2026, the Delhi High Court ordered the removal of several social media posts and videos published by the Aam Aadmi Party that allegedly depicted Chief Minister Rekha Gupta in a defamatory and demeaning way through AI-generated images and deepfake videos. The order came from Justice Manoj Jain in a defamation suit Gupta filed against the party. The posts were reported to have appeared on AAP's official and verified social media accounts. Gupta's plea asked the court to restrain the party from publishing or circulating such content.

According to the plea, the material portrayed her as a liquor vendor, hawker and delivery agent and as head of a fictitious scheme called "Har Har Rekha or Ghar Ghar Theka Yojana." One video allegedly showed her serving drinks to men at night, while another showed AI-generated figures of her and the Deputy Chief Minister pouring liquor and ice cubes. Gupta's plea said the videos looked so real that they created a misleading impression of her involvement in selling and serving liquor. The court noted that one video posted on X on November 4 had reportedly drawn about 75,000 views, 1,600 likes and 470 reposts when its screenshot was taken.

Justice Jain said that the offensive portrayal of the Chief Minister through AI-generated videos could not be treated as permissible political satire. He distinguished healthy criticism and humour from content that attacks personal dignity, and said the posts in question crossed that line by being defamatory and offensive to a woman holding constitutional office. He added that satire may hurt an individual but cannot be allowed to cause irreparable harm to dignity or reduce a person to an object of ridicule. The court also observed that holding public office invites greater scrutiny, yet does not permit the compromise of an individual's dignity.

Referring to earlier decisions, including the Raghav Chadha case, it said that until legislation regulates AI-generated content, courts must examine whether such use infringes the right to dignity. The court issued notices to all defendants, including AAP, and listed the matter for further hearing on December 4, 2026. The articles do not report any response from AAP to the order or to the allegations. They also do not say whether the content has already been removed from the platforms.

Articles.Title: Delhi HC orders takedown of AI-generated videos targeting CM Rekha Gupta

stories.Headline: NCS programme doubles reach, bringing AI and coding skills to more lower-income pupils
stories.Summary:
NCS gave more than 130 primary pupils from lower-income families hands-on lessons in artificial intelligence, coding and robotics on Oct 31 at its NCS Hub in Ang Mo Kio. The event was the largest edition yet of N-Able Me!, the company's flagship corporate social responsibility initiative, and it marked a doubling of the programme's reach in its fourth year. The pupils, all in Primary 3 to 6, took part in practical sessions rather than traditional lectures. The programme aims to narrow the digital divide by giving children from lower-income families early exposure to technology.

The curriculum included a three-hour Micro:bit workshop in which pupils learned coding basics and worked in teams to build simple games. Each participant took home a Micro:bit device to support learning beyond the event. At a Superhero AI and Robotics Booth, children used an app developed by NCS employees to create AI-generated images of themselves as superheroes pursuing their dream jobs. A 1½-hour AI masterclass introduced foundational machine learning and prompt engineering, and robotics activities let pupils see hardware engineering up close.

NCS said the programme was run by a team of company tech volunteers and supported by strategic partners including the Ministry of Social and Family Development, ComLink+, Yayasan MENDAKI and The Straits Times School Pocket Money Fund. Senior Minister of State for Social and Family Development and Home Affairs Goh Pei Ming, the guest of honour, encouraged the participants and presented them with completion certificates. Goh said that when government, community and corporate partners work together, children can be given a better start. NCS chief executive Sam Liew said technology should be an inclusive enabler whose benefits reach everyone.

The pocket money fund, started in 2000 by The Straits Times, provides financial relief to children and youth from lower-income families and has helped more than 230,000 cases to date. Under the scheme, primary pupils receive $65 a month, secondary students receive $100 a month, and those in ITEs, junior colleges and polytechnics receive $125 a month. Liew said the aim is to equip young people with foundational tools so they can see themselves as builders in the AI era. The articles do not say whether the programme will expand further or when the next edition will take place.

Articles.Title: NCS programme doubles reach, bringing AI and coding skills to more lower-income pupils

stories.Headline: Home-based patient care among AI applications being tested at next-gen 5G, 6G research centre
stories.Summary:
On November 3, 2026, the National University Health System (NUHS), telco Singtel and telecommunications equipment maker Ericsson signed a memorandum of understanding to open a research centre testing AI healthcare on 5G-Advanced and 6G networks. The centre is exploring a future in which hospital patients recovering at home are watched by wearable medical devices that detect dangerous changes, such as a sudden spike in blood pressure or an abnormal heart rate. If the readings point to an emergency, hospital staff and emergency services are alerted in real time. NUHS chief executive Yeoh Khay Guan said the partners hope to turn future telecommunications technology into practical healthcare applications. NUHS runs hospitals including National University Hospital, Ng Teng Fong General Hospital and Alexandra Hospital.

The partners say current 5G may not cope with the larger data loads expected as more patients recover at home, patient data becomes more complex and AI tools generate more data. The newer networks are expected to handle those volumes, with 5G-Advanced launched in 2025 and 6G slated for commercial launch in 2030. According to Singtel, the newer networks will be faster than current 5G and have much lower latency, meaning they respond more quickly. Chau Yuen, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University, said 6G is predicted to support a much larger number of connected devices. Because more processing can move to the cloud, devices such as augmented reality headsets could be made smaller and less bulky.

Yeoh said the planned uses include autonomous mobile robots for logistics and patient care, internet-connected devices for home care and support for surgeons during operations. NUHS plans to replace its Microsoft HoloLens headsets, which surgeons use to view a holographic image of a patient's heart from CT scans, with slimmer augmented reality glasses. Gao Yujia, director of the new National University XG AI Centre, said better networks and AI could place the hologram on a patient more accurately than is possible by hand now. Gao also said that no AI deployed on 5G so far can give hospital-wide recommendations, and that such systems have worked only at small scale, such as on a single ward. NUH is already testing nursing robots, which are meant to help nurses handle an expected rise in patient numbers rather than replace them.

Articles.Title: Home-based patient care among AI applications being tested at next-gen 5G, 6G research centre

stories.Headline: Redefining Investment Advisory in the Age of AI
stories.Summary:
On 2 November 2026, Forthright Securities, a Hong Kong brokerage under JF SmartInvest Holdings, took part in the Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK event at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre as a first-time exhibitor and Gold Sponsor. The company's pitch was that as its AI tools grow more capable, its human advisers matter more. The article is a paid post produced by the advertising partner, published on 5 November 2026, and the event opened on 2 November with more than 45,000 participants from over 120 economies. Regulators used the week to announce new measures on artificial intelligence applications and governance, tokenisation and payment connectivity.

The company's main product is the Forthright Smart Investment Terminal, a tablet aimed at experienced individual investors. It combines AI-powered analysis, real-time market support monitoring and analytical tools with the firm's investment research, while the human adviser handles questions the models cannot settle. The firm says its three most-used AI features, AI Assistant, Market Monitoring and Portfolio Analysis, have each been used by more than 80 per cent of clients. On the opening day, the Securities and Futures Commission set out plans for principles-based guidance on AI applications with greater autonomy, focused on safety and preserving human accountability and oversight.

Richard Zhengwei He, chief executive of Forthright Financial and Forthright Securities, spoke at a session titled "Agentic Alpha: The Future of Dynamic Wealth." He said agentic AI is goal-based and expects it to change how financial institutions work with clients in the short term. In the longer term, he said he sees no inherent conflict between financial institutions and agentic AI, which he described as bringing reliable, understandable and suitable guidance to people previously excluded from the financial system. Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee, speaking at the opening session, said the city has become the world's largest cross-boundary wealth hub, with net inflows to its asset and wealth management industry up roughly 200 per cent last year.

The article describes the wider context as a shift in how Hong Kong investors trade, with 95 per cent of the city's stock investors now trading online, according to the Investor and Financial Education Council's latest study. The company describes itself as a licensed brokerage that opened a four-floor flagship investor experience hub in Sheung Wan in July 2026 and gained virtual asset business qualifications in May 2026. The article does not say what the firm plans next beyond continuing to pair its AI tools with advisers. The text is promotional and carries a risk warning stating that AI analyses are for reference only and do not constitute investment advice.

Articles.Title: Redefining Investment Advisory in the Age of AI

stories.Headline: Anthropic: CLAUDE.md Rules Are Requests; Hooks Are Enforced
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's guide to Claude Code, read on November 8, 2026, draws a line between instructions the model may ignore and rules the software enforces. Addy Osmani, who works on Claude Code, repeated the same split in an X article posted that day. The guide says that prompts, CLAUDE.md files and skills are requests that Claude can decline to follow. It says hooks, deny rules and managed settings are applied by Claude Code every time, regardless of what the model decides.

The guide's practical advice follows from that split. If something has to happen every time, it should be built as a hook, a deny rule or a managed setting rather than written as a sentence in CLAUDE.md. The guide describes CLAUDE.md as the place for guidelines that Claude may decide do not apply. It also lists seven older habits it says users can drop, including writing rules in capital letters, telling the model not to be lazy and asking it to think harder.

In the guide's view, emphatic phrasing tends to make Claude over-apply a rule, and pushing for more effort often causes overwork rather than fixing a stall. The guide is Anthropic's own documentation, and Osmani's article applies the same reasoning in his own words. Osmani advises that after two failed corrections, a user should clear the session and write a better prompt, since further corrections pile onto a conversation the model keeps re-reading. He also coins two terms for problems he sees in practice: an "orchestration tax" when many agents at once demand more attention, and "code ratification" when large changes are approved only because tests pass.

The guide adds limits of its own, saying a WebFetch deny rule for a domain does not stop curl reaching that domain unless the sandbox is enabled, and that auto mode relies on a classifier model rather than a hard rule. The articles do not say how often instructions in CLAUDE.md are ignored in real use, and they do not report any tests of the enforced controls. Both sources describe how the controls are meant to work. Anthropic's documentation can change over time, so the guide's current wording may differ from the version read here.

Articles.Title: Anthropic: CLAUDE.md Rules Are Requests; Hooks Are Enforced - FourWeekMBA

stories.Headline: Las Vegas students share bold perspectives on democracy, AI and privacy at Sun Youth Forum
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 3, 2026, about 700 juniors and seniors from across the Clark County School District gathered at Cimarron-Memorial High School for the annual Las Vegas Sun Youth Forum. The students broke into small, diverse groups to debate immigration reform, opioid addiction, Flock cameras, artificial intelligence, and the future of the Republican Party. The forum has run since 1956, with cancellations only in 2020 and 2021 because of the pandemic. Tuesday also happened to be Election Day, when many of the students' parents and other adults were voting in the midterms.

Sun publisher and editor Brian Greenspun told the students that by analyzing difficult issues they were taking part in democracy, even though most were too young to vote. He said that in five years or ten years, the lessons from the forum would help them handle public responsibilities more effectively. Before the discussions wrapped up, he announced $37,000 in scholarships for attendees. The forum was started by founding Sun publisher Hank Greenspun, his assistant Ruthe Deskin, and Clark County School District administrator Harvey Dondero, who believed students deserved to be heard as well as seen.

In one group, Joey Morehouse, a student at Southwest Career and Technical Academy, said young people in Las Vegas have communities but few places to gather, especially for the independent music scene he belongs to. He said affordable all-ages venues have been pushed into parts of the valley that teens avoid out of fear of violence, and that many musicians under 21 cannot perform on Fremont Street. Another group was skeptical of Flock cameras, and Coronado High School student Frankie Catanzaro compared them to the surveillance in George Orwell's "1984." She argued the cameras do more than read license plates and invade privacy. In a third room, Desert Oasis High School student Edward Longbardi questioned whether the Republican Party's next leader had emerged yet, even as the group favored Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The articles do not describe any formal outcome, policy change, or follow-up beyond the forum itself. The students' highlights were to be presented to the wider community, with participants writing columns for the Sun or being interviewed on UNLV-TV or KUNV radio. The articles also note that Democrats won the midterms in Nevada and nationally, taking majorities in both chambers of Congress, the same day the forum took place. The closing discussion on universal human experiences produced answers ranging from death and grief to love and hate.

Articles.Title: Las Vegas students share bold perspectives on democracy, AI and privacy at Sun Youth Forum - Las Vegas Sun

stories.Headline: Opinion: College dual enrollment programs risk fueling a high school AI arms race
stories.Summary:
Michael Walsh, an affiliated faculty member at the University of Alaska Anchorage, published an opinion piece in the Anchorage Daily News on November 8, 2026, arguing that colleges should rethink how they choose students for dual enrollment programs. He says that selection criteria such as class rank, grade point average and prerequisite courses are now distorted by students using artificial intelligence chatbots on their schoolwork. The piece frames this as a risk that high school students will feel pressure to use AI more heavily to stay competitive, creating what he calls an AI arms race. He notes that the article is an opinion and that its claims come from his own reasoning and research he cites.

Walsh says colleges and universities should adjust their criteria so that dual enrollment placement reflects students' readiness for college coursework rather than work that may be done with chatbot help. He suggests one option is requiring a minimum score on a proctored, closed-book selection exam. He also proposes a widely adopted national blue-ribbon standard that would let the public tell apart programs that select students on readiness alone. He argues such a mark would give institutions more reason to change their criteria, since few would act alone if competitors did not.

Walsh places responsibility on several groups, including parents, secondary school administrators and teachers, and college administrators and professors. He argues that these groups are judged and rewarded on short-term measures, such as the number of dual enrolled students, which discourages them from enforcing rules on AI use. He also points to the revenue that dual enrollment brings to some colleges and the political weight that state and local officials have placed on these programs as alternatives to Advanced Placement courses. He cites a Pew Research Center survey showing that a majority of U.S. teens use AI chatbots for schoolwork, and a recent study suggesting that students who rely on AI perform worse on learning and retention once the tools are removed. The article does not describe any next steps by institutions or policymakers.

Articles.Title: Opinion: College dual enrollment programs risk fueling a high school AI arms race - Anchorage Daily News

stories.Headline: AI stock rout: Should Singapore investors buy the dip or cut exposure?
stories.Summary:
A sharp sell-off in US technology stocks has spread to Asia and Singapore, leaving investors to weigh whether to buy the dip, cut their exposure or wait. The Nasdaq 100 plunged 6.4% on Nov 5, two days after the US midterm elections, wiping out about US$2.5 trillion in market value. The S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank 12.2%. Chip-heavy markets in South Korea, Taiwan and Japan were hit on Nov 6, and Singapore-listed technology stocks also took a beating.

The fall followed a Democratic sweep of Congress, which raised the prospect of tighter scrutiny of artificial intelligence. Investors were already questioning how quickly spending on chips and data centres would turn into profits, and experts said crowded AI bets and borrowed money may have amplified the drop as funds rushed for the exits. Investors are watching whether greater scrutiny of electricity and water use, grid costs and permits leads to rules that delay data centre construction. They are also looking at whether major cloud providers trim their spending plans and whether chipmakers cut their earnings forecasts.

Saxo chief investment strategist Charu Chanana said in a note to investors on Nov 6 that AI demand and existing infrastructure had not disappeared overnight, and that many leading technology companies still have substantial cash flows and competitive advantages. She described the change as one in market sentiment and in how investors judge future growth, regulatory risk and acceptable valuations. Brian Levitt, chief global market strategist at Invesco, called the sell-off a reset in one of the market's most crowded trades, warning the correction could continue. He also said lower prices are making some AI stocks more attractive to long-term investors.

Chanana advised that long-term investors who can ride out further losses may keep investing regularly if their holdings still suit them. She suggested those with spare cash focus on firms with strong balance sheets, steady cash flow and reasonable valuations, and spread purchases over time. Heavily exposed investors could shift money towards established cash-generating businesses or other sectors, while those trading on margin should work out how far prices could fall before they must add cash or sell. Afdhal Rahman, executive director of wealth advisory at OCBC, said in a Nov 6 note that cloud giants such as Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon are relatively well placed in the near term, while he favours graphics processors, custom chips and networking equipment. He was more cautious about smaller AI cloud providers that rely heavily on debt.

Articles.Title: AI stock rout: Should Singapore investors buy the dip or cut exposure?

stories.Headline: Japan deploys AI, specialist teams to counter cyberattack wave
stories.Summary:
Japan's government on Friday, November 6, 2026, approved a package of emergency measures after a run of personal data breaches caused by unauthorised access. The package was announced at a meeting of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and relevant ministers. It was drawn up after Takaichi asked officials the previous week to prepare it, following a series of high-profile leaks from cyberattacks. One of those attacks hit the internet service provider GMO Internet Group, which was faced with a ransom demand. Public concern about cybersecurity has been rising in the same period.

The package calls for more use of artificial intelligence to find weaknesses in computer systems. It also provides for setting up several teams of highly skilled specialists. According to the report, a rescue team drawn from experts in the public and private sectors will be formed to help businesses hit by cyberattacks with their initial responses. The articles do not give a budget, a headcount or a start date for these teams. They also do not say how the new teams will coordinate with existing agencies.

The articles do not identify any party held responsible for the breaches beyond the attackers, and they do not name any company that failed to protect data. Prime Minister Takaichi is described as having directed officials to produce the package and as leading the meeting where it was announced. The report attributes the measures to the government as a whole, which compiled them with the relevant ministries. Kyodo, the news agency that reported the story, is the named source of the account.

The package responds to a wave of cyberattacks that has drawn attention to Japan's defences, and the articles tie it directly to that wave. The report does not describe what the government will do next or set out a timeline for implementing the measures. It also does not say whether further legislation or funding will follow. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Japan deploys AI, specialist teams to counter cyberattack wave

stories.Headline: Europe’s AI Stocks Are Falling. Is the Selloff Overdone?
stories.Summary:
Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence boom fell sharply on Thursday and Friday, November 5 and 6, 2026, after Democrats won broadly in the U.S. midterm elections. The Nasdaq Composite had its deepest one-day drop in 19 months on Thursday, with the Nasdaq losing more than 5%, and the rout wiped nearly $3 trillion off the market value of S&P 500 companies. On Friday, markets in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan were hit hard, and the Korea Exchange imposed a circuit breaker in morning trading after the KOSPI fell 8.7% at one point. Investors worried that Democratic control of Congress, including wins in some key data-center states, could bring tougher AI regulation and slow the construction of data centers. The selling had started before the election, as chipmakers and neocloud companies helped drive the Nasdaq to its worst October since March 2025.

The drop confirmed the Nasdaq Composite was in correction territory and put it on track for a fourth straight weekly fall. The CBOE Volatility Index logged its biggest one-day jump in about 19 months and stood at 26.07 on Friday. Nvidia had its largest one-day fall since January 2025, when the Chinese model DeepSeek rattled Wall Street, though it rose 3.6% in premarket trading on Friday. Other chip stocks, including AMD, Intel, Broadcom and Micron Technology, were up between 5% and 8.3% in premarket trading. Nasdaq 100 futures were up 1.48% at 4:14 a.m.

ET, while Dow futures were down 0.66%. Anthropic, the AI company preparing to go public, felt the effects directly. CNBC reported that some of its investors had lowered their valuation hopes, with one saying a more likely range was $1 trillion to $1.25 trillion. That compares with a $1.5 trillion figure another investor called a stretch and a recent target of $2 trillion. The investors spoke anonymously because they were not authorized to discuss the matter, and Anthropic declined to comment.

Analyst Gil Luria of D.A. Davidson said investors would expect the deal to price at least at the low end of earlier expectations, and that pricing it well was the best way to set the company up for success. Jane Gibbons, an equity strategist at Jefferies, described Thursday's selloff as reactionary rather than a fundamental reset, driven by worries over AI spending, policy and inflation. Anthropic filed its registration statement on October 26, 2026, and an amended preliminary prospectus on November 2 seeks a listing on the Nasdaq Global Select Market, with the share count and price range still undetermined. The filing shows $17.0 billion of revenue for the three months ended September 30, 2026, up 1,127% from a year earlier, while compute and infrastructure expenses grew 382%.

It also discloses roughly $895.4 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements, about $69.8 billion of which falls due within twelve months. The company had raised $141.1 billion in total and held $95.6 billion in cash, plus $36.3 billion in short-term investments. Its roadshow was still expected to begin in the week of November 9, and a May 28 round had valued it at $965 billion. Meanwhile, an October jobs report due Friday could shape interest-rate expectations, with traders pricing a more than 65% chance of a December hike.

Articles.Title: Japan, South Korea stocks plummet as AI selloff accelerates

stories.Headline: How Singapore confronts AI fears of ‘broken’ career ladder, no pause button
stories.Summary:
Singapore is trying to turn its land and manpower limits into a reason to embrace artificial intelligence rather than fear it, according to a senior official speaking in Hong Kong. The technology carries the risk of job losses and cyberthreats if it falls into the wrong hands. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo made these remarks at the Family Business Summit on Wednesday, an event co-organised by the South China Morning Post and Blue Pool Capital. Her comments were reported by Kolette Lim in an article published on November 6, 2026.

Teo argued that a pragmatic approach would give the resource-scarce country an advantage. She said Singapore should avoid becoming overly reliant on any single power or any single AI provider. She also outlined five imperatives that guide the country's AI policy. Her warning centred on the pace of change, since AI was advancing faster than societies could adapt. She cautioned that younger workers could face a "broken rung" on the career ladder as businesses shifted spending from wages toward AI technology.

Teo's position, as the article presents it, is that the risks of AI cannot be paused and must instead be managed through pragmatic policy. The article does not describe any specific new law, budget figure or deadline attached to her remarks. It also does not say how the government plans to address the entry-level job squeeze she described. The report frames her comments as a response to a broader public anxiety about AI's effect on careers and security. Further policy details beyond her speech are not given in the article.

Articles.Title: How Singapore confronts AI fears of ‘broken’ career ladder, no pause button

stories.Headline: Taiwan, South Korea, Japan stock markets hit hard by AI sell-off
stories.Summary:
Asian stock markets tied to the artificial intelligence boom fell sharply on Friday, November 6, 2026, after a tech sell-off on Wall Street overnight. Investors in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan sold off AI-linked shares as the selling spread through the region. The article reports that the Korea Exchange imposed a circuit breaker during morning trading to slow the decline, after the KOSPI fell 8.7% at one point. The article is dated November 6, 2026, and was updated later that day.

The sell-off followed a sweeping Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections, which raised concerns about possible delays in the construction of data centers. Investors feared that new scrutiny of AI, and possible curbs on data center development, could slow the spending that has driven the sector. The article notes that the concern was strong enough to pull down markets across the region in a single session. It does not give details of any specific new rule or legislation that has been passed.

The article also points to related coverage in the same publication, including a report that Nasdaq plunged 5.5% amid AI regulation fears, and FX traders' view that a Democratic "blue wave" could support the yen if the AI trade reverses. Other linked pieces cover U.S. tech companies' growing AI-related debt and Anthropic's plan to seek up to $3.5 billion from Japanese investors in an IPO. The article itself does not name a specific official or company as responsible for the decline. Beyond these reports, the available material does not say how long the sell-off lasted or what policy steps may follow.
